As we.deseende there was a crash • of glass and the fall of a hard body as if asstone had been thrown through the window. ,The dining-loom, as the Sokiree of the noise, was our first care. • Entering cautiously we found the chairs in disorder, eatables scattered, decanters up set, •'a broken pane is the French • window, but 11,, trace of the alissile we bad heard falling! There was silence while George and 1 armed ourselves with the weapons .of the fireside. Then our hair bristled ..or we heard in the library, which opened off this oom, a scuffle, a blow, a thud, and a faint moan! While we stood petrified there eame'from the halha sound as if something was being dragged towards the drawing room door. We rustled into the library—nothing wrong ap, paroutly—no onei visible. I stepped forward, :mit recoiled in tiorror, for Ihad.wet my stockinged tot in a dark red peel that lay beside Hepworth's library ciiair There Was 81)11)6.'11pol. left in the decanters and we "fortified "'before attacking the drawing-ruoin where we knew the enemy to be hidden, That. blood and the "dragging" sound that nearly done fur us.

Meanwhile the enemy were silent. But as entered the hall, •a wild horrid discord rang out fromtle piano, followed by a scudid and a Jap or two. 'e .PO.llBO-01014 shoving each, other along, IVO landed all together in the drawing room—and a 1 covered withy Hgooge-skiii." k . spa tab • drawing room, It!. :dearly 'visible, was ,empty, and undisturbed. 110 curtains . hung fiat— no one hidden there. The piano stood open aa it was left with Jessie's shawl in a heap on the corner —but no fleshly performer was there. . This began to seem worse than burglar& .We sidled towards the piano—Hepworth raised his lamp—and then an av:in! hiny happened. The shawl was lifted bodily by some invisible force, and hurled Straight at the lamp cx- tmguishing it with a crash of the chimney—and then falling on the floor "with the futUie blow, thud, and .11,i:fa we had heard, iii Ike library and which certainly ,!aniii from no material source!

ilepworth tired instinctively and we retreated with uncontrollable cries of horror—for .now we knew that we lied been face to face with no mortal visitant. The scuttling and knocking were re- peated for a second or two, but nothing followed us. The first necessity was to hurriedly "fortify " again—the second, to re-assure the hysterical women upstairs who naturally thought there had been serious casualities. We brought them down to the dining room now that the burglar theory Nro3 exploded—and told ihem our blood-curdling experi- ences. After that, even our blue ribbonites did unit refuse a little spiritual comfort. And it was then that we first noticed something ominous. "llerr Greybeard" was gone! He had not been knocked off the table or upset—for neither he, nor any spilt Milk, lay on the floor—lie had simply vanished! A chill ran through ine'sts I thought IA his mysterious history and his fancied leer. What mediaival spell lay upon him? Of what malignant personality was be the instrument? _ _

We men soon deeide,l that, under the wgis of our womenkind, WC •con even face the drawing room again. We did, with all the lamps we could carry, alld found it exactly in statu quo with one awful exception. The shawl had disappeared. • We shrank back an instant, and then resolved that we would find that shawl if we had to move every piece of furniture in the room. Soon there was a good imitation of an auction room in the middle of the floor—but no shawl. " Como boys," said Hepworth, "there's nothing left but that corm! e Homan. If it's not there, it's gone to sheol. (hop- orth's whisk?y was seven years old.) Out calve Lhe ottoman—anl there lay the shawl Hesitatingly he stopped—pulled at a corner of it—and sprang back— "My God—it's as heavy as lead 1 " A shuddering phase, and then—" Well we'll have it out anyhow! ' A jerk—a thump—a rumble—and out it Caine. And out of it rolled, Herr Greybeard —with the same leer on his face that I bad tam:led before!

And then there burst from all our throats an un- controllable shriek—for Herr Greybeard was not alone—he brought with him a body I But it was a shriek of wild laughter for the "body" was the body of a eat! l'oor pussy had got her head jammed in his narrow neck while try- ing to gets drank, and was now, after so maily fir. ful antics, stone dead, droal.ta in the milk she lied tried to steal! We need not explain the "manifestations detail. Anyone who knows the ways of a cat with her head stuck fast in a pitcher that wont break, can till in the particulars. If she jumped on the piano and got tangled in that shawl, she might have lived to explain it all herself. But the pool of blood r Well, I thought of that myself, and hurried into the library. where I stubbed my toe against the heavy bottle that used, 'o hold the purple copying ink. As for the "pungent, depressing smell,' we found, that the back damper of the halt stove has bee* elosed too tightly, so it was only coal gas after all. And the stolen money? Why or that was in Depworth's pocket-book, in llie breast-pocket of his overcoat. And his overcoat was where it should be—on the clothes rack in the lieu. As wa argued about the NJ'. all the way borer the night before, it was no wonder he had forgotten to tato the cash up. stairs. We breakfasted rather !ale on New Year's Day, and felt rather seedy. And we had plenty of things to talk over among ourselves and with the married daughters, though neither Mrs. Katie nor Mrs. Maggie, nor their husbands, had any similar tale of ghostly yisiiations to relaW. So Jessie and I agreed that we would not dare to face another New Year's Eve without that protec- tion against the "powers of the air" which matri- *may evidently if

RAILWAY ACCIDENT,—When the eight o'clock train from Liverpool arrived at Priscot on Mrnday evening it was found that one of the cylinders bad burst. An engine was wired tor from St. Helens and after a delay of about 22 minutes the train proceed to Wigan, and arrived there without any further accident.

Tun WATBR SUPPLY.—The Rev. T. Chambers gave no- tice that at the next meeting of the Board he would raise the question of the water supply to the workhouse. This was the principal business. THE WATCH TRADE: PUBLIC MUTING. On Wednesday night a public meeting, under the aus- pices of the Preecot Watch Trade Association, was bold in the Town Hall, Prescot, to receive a report from the depu- tation which recently waited upon the Board of Trade with reference to the depression in the watch trade. The meson's- tion was established in April last, and its objects are stated to be "to unite the various branches of the English watch trade, so that they can act in concert to remove any evils from which the trade may suffer and to adopt inch mea- sures as will tend to preserve the watchmaking industry." Considering that watchmaking is the principal industry of Prescot, and that foreign imitations are causing great depres- sion in the Irmo, the attendance was small, not more than from thirty to forty persons being present. Mr. William Tyrer presided, and was supported by Messrs. James Berry, T. P. Hewitt, and J. Robinson (secretary.) The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said that one of the objects of the meeting was le form a permanent as- sociation for protecting the interests of the trade, and to remedy, if possible, some of the evils from which it was at present suffering. (Applause.) The Secretary, in presenting a report of the proceedings of the committee of the association, said that aeon the 25th of last month it was ascertained that the Board of Trade were engaged in framing a fraudulent marks bill, the trade deemed it a seasonable opportunity to press their claims upon the Government, and the result was that a conference was held in I,ondon and a deputation waited upon Lord Stanley. Thla cotandttee in their action hail met with criticism in various fermi. It was stated that one TOSIOII if the destine in the watch trade was that the Swiss watches were so much superior and so much better designed than the English. If that were so, he should like to ask why the Beim copied English designs, and also why they did not go abroad, their own coat, and not put on the coat of the Britishers, and parade it up and down as their own manu- facture. (Applause.) All the watch industry of Great Britain asked for wee a fair field and no favour. Foreigners had every facility offered to them to pass their own goods as British manufacture, and to take the watchmaking industry out of this eonahry. (Applause.) Mr. J. Berry, one of the deputation to the soaferenee in Lotdon and to the Board Of Trade, gave a brief name of what took plain cm those ateasions, as recently reported in the public prints. In *minding, be remarked that he was sure that it they mould get the Legislature to move in the desired direction they wined see the trade of Promos good, and the whole of the town well emplOyed. (applause.) Mr. W. Lloyd moved, and Mr. W. Brown seeended, the following revolution :—"Tbat, in the °pillion of this moo- ing, She OOMmitiee of the Presaot Watch Trade Amoebae* have edited wisely la sending representatives to the OP eta- am of the valeh tide held ia London on the 14th inst., and it is loped that the representatives will eoutinne to set in unison, so that the heedulent praetieee of vitteh the trade somplaht may be temoved." (Near, hear.) The resolution was entried unanimouely. I Mr. Hewitt proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Hartley ' Work to the ?retool Colon) for his services in eoaneetion with drawing op a memorial to the Board of Trade relating to the watchmaking industry which he had transmitted to all the Boards of Guardians in Great Britain. The vote of I thanks also included thanks to the Prescot Board of Gnar- -1 diens, and particularly Mr. C. B. Johnson and Mr. Tyrer, members of the Board, for the trouble they had taken in the matter.
Mr. Dyson seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. J. Case, and married unanimously. Totes of thanks were acoordel to Alessi'. Berry, Hewitt, and Robinson, the deputation to London.

When the house was broken into on lnesday afternoon two women named Welch were found dead from suffocation, so that four lives have been lost.

FATAL ICE ACC (DlE:lr.—About four o'clock on Sunday afternoon a shocking ice accident occurred at Bolton. A young man named Marsden, aged 18, gallantly went into a mill lodge to rescue a man named Thompson, who was drowning, when he fell through, and was drowned be- fore assistance arrived. Thompson was afterwards rescued with a clothes line, and the body of Marsden was recovered by the police. lan BIiLFAST RIOTS.—It is stated that in the report which they are about to present the Commissioners who sat to inquire into the circumstances of the Belfast riots will, among other things, reccommend "the effacement of the local justices from the bench," the appointment of lawyers as resident magistrates, and the suppression of party pre- cessions. The Commissioners, it is added, will express ap- proval of the action of the constabulary. SUICIDE OF A PAUPER THROUGH LONE.—OR Sunday the body of Richard Larkin, aged 23, was found in a pit near Fishpool Warkhouse, Bolton. Larkin has been a pauper in- mate of the workhouse almost all his life. On the Bth No- vember he sent two notes to an assistant pupil teacher there declaring his love. The matter was reported to the guar- diem, and Larkin was punished. Immediately afterwards he left the workhouse without permission, and was not seen again until his body was found on Sunday. DESTRUGTIVE SNOWSTORM.

TELEGRAPHIC AND RAILWAY COMMUNICA- • TION INTERRUPTED. Sow, commenced falling in London about six o'clock on Sunday evening, with every prospect of , its 'continuing throughout the night. Notwith- standing that there had been rain throughout the 1 day the snow accumulated. In South Somerset and I other parts snow fell heavily. Owing doubtless, to I the heavy snowstorm in the south, there was a complete breakdown of all telegraphic communica- tion on Sunday night, not a single wire being avail- I able between London and Lancashire after ten I L o'clock. The storm was the most,. severe that has I been witnessed in the Metropolis for many yearsl past: The fall has been computed at 14 inches; but the drifts in many-places were fully six feet. On, ; Monday, traffic was almost at a standstill, Efforts ' ! were made to clear away the snow, but with little result for some hours. The damage Caused by thei high wind, following the heavy fall, is almost meal- culable. Hoardings, chimney stacks, exposed walls, and trees suffered severely; but without doubt the greatest damage was done to the overhead telegraph wires. Throughout the city these lay in all dime- tions. Some of .the telegraph 'posts, snapped off short, swayed in the wind high overhead, while in other places bunches of thirty wires lay broken in .the road in Cornhill, Caurion-street,,and Coleman- street. St. Paul's Churchyard, where the wires are especially thick, the damage done was exceptionally great. With the railway companies, this wholesale destruction of wires proved a very serious calamity: No signals coUld be transmitted, and all trains were sent through by hand signals, the delay being very considerable. The Telegraph Department gave notice that all telegraphic work would be delayed in con- sequence of the broken wires: • •• • • • In the grounds of Buckingham Palace the stbrm did great damage. The havoc-played innOng the elms is described as fearful. In consequence-91 the heavy snowstorm south of tirmingliam, cotamimi- cation with London,- east, south-east; south, and south-west and west was considerably interrupted. The submarine company gave notice of total inter- ruption to the continent. English land lines of the Eastern Indo-European, direct Spanish, Great Northern, and all American cable companies, were also interrupted, and serious delay ensued. Tele- graphic communication was totally interrupted with a large part of the kingdom on Monday, and there was a great delay to the remainder. Owing to the breakdown of the telegraphic service a col- lision occurred on Monday on the South-Eastern Railway at Beckenham. From 20 to 30 passengers were more or less seriously shaken, and Mr. Bagg, of North Croydon, was seriously injured about the head, and removed to hospital. Between 30 and 40 persons were admitted to the Leeds Infirm- ary suffering from injuries caused by slippery pave- meat.

Some fatal shipping casualties are reported. Early on Monday morning the Trixie West, of Folkestone, was seen in distress off Morpensess. While her crew were being rescued by the rocket apparatus a schooner was seen a ihore a little to the north- ward. For some hours efforts to save the crew were fruitless, but eventually they were taken off by the Dunwich and Code Exchange lifeboats, with the exception of one man, who was drowned. This vessel was the Day Star, of Ipswich. To the north of this wreck, a vessel believed to be the lAagnet got ashore, and only one man was saved. If is thought the cap- tain's wife was on board. Three bodies were washed ashore. For some miles along the coast wreckage is being washed ashore. Two schooners are reported to have come into collision off Southwold, where also considerable damage was done to shipping. A Lloyd's telegram states that the British steamer Effective arrived at Madeira on Monday having on board the crew of the British steamer Tourmaline, from Cardiff for St. Lucia, which vessel was aban- doned on the 24th. inst. 180 miles north-west of Madeira. The Tourmaline was an iron screw steamer of 2,043 gross tons, built at Stockton in 1883, and owned by Messrs. Christie and Co., Cardiff. More . details are to hand from the snow-bound districts, showing the severity of Sunday's storm. Devizes (Wilts) has been isolated since Sunday. The first train proceeded six miles, when it stuck fast in a drift. The engine fire went out, and the guard walked back to Devizes. At Brixham, heavy rains flooded the town, causing the main sewer to burst. The gasworks were flooded, the fires extinguished, and the town was thus placed in total darkness. The Baptist Chapel was also flooded, stopping divine service. The harbour lights were extin- guished, and much anxiety was felt for about 100 fishing smacks which were in the outer harbour, and exposed to the gale. GALE IN THE CHANNEL. _ _

CALA/8, MONDAY NIGHT.— A terrible hurricane has been blowing here since fcur o'clock this morn- ing. No boat has yet arrived from Dover. The steamer Petrel left at 1-50 p.m„ with 30 passengers for Dover.

A Lloyd's telegram from Hurst Castle, dated Tues- day afternoon, says the Royal Mail Company's steamer Medway, from the West Indies, &c., with passengers and cargo for Southampton, went ashore at Yarmouth, Isle of Wight. about midnight Tugs are in attendance, and she will probably soon float. • telegram dated Cowes, Tuesday morning, says that the Medway lies on an even keel and good bottom, off Boulder (Tarmouth). The position is sheltered, but the vessel will probably have to be lightened. The tugs which were sent from South- ampton on Monday morning at high water, to at- tempt to assist the Medway off, were unsuccessful In their efforts, and returned to Southampton in the evening with the Medway's specie. ~The mails had been landed at Plymouth. The schooner Leila, from Newport tor Norway with eoal, was run into on Tuesday morning by the steamer Alaerity, of Cardiff, and went down ten mi- nutes after the collision. The master, and two of the crew were drowned.

div.head: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION AT BIRKEN-
div.p: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION AT BIRKEN-

HEAD. FIVE LIVES LOST. Alt explosion of petroleum gas in the hold of the steamer Petriana, lying in N 0.3 graving dock of the ship repairing yard of Messrs. Glover and Company, of Birkenhead, on Sunday, caused the deaths of Ave men and injury to five others. The Petriana, which is seven years old, is an iron vessel of about 1,100 tons burden. The hold had been recently converted into a number of tanks to enable the vessel to carry petroleum in bulk from Batoum, on the Black Sea, she being the first vessel specially fitted up for this trade. The steamer arrived in the Mersey a few days ago, with a cargo of 2,000 tone of petroleum in bulk, this being her first voyage in the trade. On her passage to Liverpool she encountered the full force of the recent storms, and suffered very severely, and had her decks smashed, severals boats washed away, the bridge smashed and damaged, and, in addition to other parts being damaged, was severely strained in the hold. The consequence of this straining was that the petroleum in 3ne of the tanks 'was found to be leaking into the water-tank underneath it. The vessel has six tanke---three for- ward and three aft. On arriving in the Mersey she was taken to the Herculaneum Dock, where the cargo was discharged; and in order to have the damage done by the storm made good, the vessel was on Saturday morning towed into the graving dock. To execute the repairs with speed, an extra staff of riveters, caulkers, and others were put to work in the tank, the work proceeaing, day and night. When the repairs were completed it was de- cided that a thorough investigation should be made, and several of Messrs. Glover's workmen and others went into one of the forward tanks with naked lights. Besides the workmen there were in the tank during the inspection Captain Enright, the master of the steamer; Mr. Mayor; Mr. Ernest A. Fawcns, of the firm of Messrs. Flannery and Fawcus, consult- ing engineers, Liverpool; Mr. William James, for- merly boiler maker to Messrs. Clayton and Co.;"and Mr. Allison, superintendent engineer to the owners of the Petriana. The tank in which they were is 30ft. long by 30ft. high, and 34ft. wide, and under- neath this is the water compartment, which was filled for the purposs of testing whether the leak had been stopped. Shortly after the party had gone into the tank, a fearful explosion occurred, followed by a great volume of !lame rushing out of the deck hatchway leading into the tank, and the air was filled with a cloud of smoke and the fumes of gas. The workmen in the yard ran to the vessel, and were horrified to Seeseveral men coming from the Ii atchway with their clothing in flames. Assistance was ren- dered to them as speedily as possible, and after the fire in their clothing had been extinguished, they were conveyed to the Borough Hospital in cabs. When it was discovered that four of those who were known to have gone into the hold were miss- ing, an attempt was made to try to render them some assistance, in the hope that they might be still living. In this, however, the willing workers were baffled, fot the hold was so full ot smoke that it was impossible for anyone to go down. It was ul- timately decided to procure the services of a diver, and about nine o'clock, Walter Lawrence, diver, des- cended into the tank, and in about an hour brought

NEW BOOKS, eze. The Lancashire Christmas Annual, published by Ms. John Heywood, has reached the fifth year of its existence; and, as it is a good eixpenny-worth, it is likely to have a long career. Is is illustraited, sad the stories and sketches are ratty and interestian. " Diproses Annual" attracts attention on the book eel's by its brilliant cover, and its three typical heads of England, Scotland, and. Ireland. There is a baker's dozen of stories, all of which are well written; and most of them are adopted by full-page illustra- tions. The opening tale, "A Slave of the Poppy," is a revelation as to the baneful effeete sof opium setae which will not be without its value as a werniag at the present day. "Madame Tabby's Establiahmenn" by Said, is a new volume from the press of Messrs. Xaomillaia and Co. It is a cat story of on extreordiaary kind, and it is skilfully illustrated by Mr. L. Wale, who has a faculty for giving expression to the characteris- tics of pussy. The story is in a lively vein all through, and there is somethiag origiaal awl speeial- ly attractive in treating an establishment of cats se having in many respects the charsoteristios of human beings. Madame Tabby has quite as mush trouble with her numerous kittens as has any Madame in the land who has charge of a large private school for girls. Then there is a King of the Cats, with a dee- oriptiou of Court life wheo . has special reference to the lively doings of Princes Jumpy Wunipy. It is im- possible for the elders wko re&d. this book not to per- ceive that there is a good deal of pungent satire in "Madame Tabby's Establishment" on "the way we live now." The young people will run through the work in their liking for the story, which is altogether novel, and capitally told. "Honour is my Guise" is the title of the latest issue of Messrs. Cas.sell's "golden mottoes " series. It is from the pen of a matured writer, Jeanie Hering (Mr. Adams-Anton), author of "Golden Days," "Truth will out," &0., and it is admirably illustrated by W. S. Stacey. The story extends to over twenty chapters, and every chapter is interesting. It is dif- ficult to write with a moral purpose without becoming distasteful; but the author has so accomplished the task, that the young, for whom this book is more es- pecially written, will enjoy themselves in reading the tale as one which is good Without being goody- goody." The various characters are well and firmly drawn; it is real life which is being described, and the trials and troubles are of that every-day kind which nobody escapes. We can strongly recommend "Honour is my guide" as a piece of reallywholesome literature. No boy or girl could read the story with- out feeling stimulated to higher moral activity, The ideal is high, but not too high for attain• ment. The second part is to hand of Bainee's History of Lancashire, as edited and extended by Mr. James Credo's, F.S.A., and printed and published by Mr. John Heywood. It contains a map of Lancashire according to the Domesday survey of 1086, with the original spelling—Warrington, for instance, figuring as Walinstone. Referring to the Lancashire pert of Domesday Book, the editor says—" We give the translation as made from a careful examination of the fee-simile by W. Beamont, Eel, of Orford Hall, Warrington, in his Literal Extension and Transla- tion of Domesday Book—Cheshire and Lancashire, &0., and by his permission." These is a fine en- graving on page 68 of John of Gannt's Gateway, Lancaster Castle. It will thus be seen thtt the cur- rent issue is of special interest. Messrs. Scribner and Sons, New York, are making a bold venture in issuing " Scribner's Magazine." It will be remembered that the original "Scribner" was merged in "The Century," so that the new magazine is a distinct addition to this class of literature. The first number promises well. It opens with a deeply interesting paper " Reminiseencea of the Siege and Commune of Paris," by Mr. G. B. Washburne, who, as the American Minister, at that time, to Franca writes as an eye-witness, and with special knowledge, from the most authoritative sources. Amongst the , illustrations must be mentioned a capital pot trait of the late M., Gambetta. The following articles are also illustrated:—" The Story of New 'Ptak Howie ; " "Our Defenceless Coasts ; " "The Babylonian .Seals;" and "Glimpses of the Diaries of Gouverneur Morris." There is, too, a good supply of fiction and verse, and as theprioe of the magazine is one ehilling only, it is sure to have an enormous sale. Messrs. F. Warne and Co. are the English publishers. "Swiss Family Robinson," that classic for the young second only to "Robinson Crusoe," has been newly translated and issued, in handsome book form by Mr. John Heywood, Manchester and London. The new edition is edited by Aifonzo Gardiner, who ,has done a considerable amount of judicious pruning in order to bring the science and natural history down to date. Care has, of course, been taken not to inter- fere with the story. In, fact it gains rather than loses by treatment of this kind, for story books Must not be.too much overlaid with instruction, or they 'will not be read. It is a good idea, therefore, te give the special notate; history information in the shape of notes. The youthful reader will probably in the first inetance pass them over until he has finished reading the tale.. He will then probably turn to the notes. without feeling that they are in the way. The nett edition- is profusely illustrated and tastefully bound, and is just the sort of book to place in the hands of a boy or girl-as a New Year's present, " °aspire Magazine" for January commences the year in good style. There is it paper on "How to be Happy though mons " by the author of "How to be happy. though married ''; the Family Doctor treats of Food for Invalids; there are more hints about art- istic furniture; with Letters from the Planets, and eeveral stories besides the two serial stories. ' In the interest of American subscribers to the magazine, a special American competition is announced, a prize being given for the best paper on "The Domestic Service Difficulty in America." In the current issue of "The Quiver" the same matter is touched upon as it relates to this country under the title of "Au order of Honourable Service.' The editor proposes to enrol and give prizes to servants who have maintained irre- proachable rectitude of character in the service of one family for not less than seven years, It is a god idea to make "An order of Honourable Service." Amongst other notable papers in this month's " Quiver " should be mentioned" A Sandwich supper in seven Dials,' "Charles Wesley and Marylebone," " A Century of Hussars," and "Our New Testa- ment Names and whet they teach." Their is a full supply of " short arrows" too, and they all hit the mark. "Little Folks" for January has 'for frontie- niece a very pretty rdoture in colours, "Their little Queen "—which is in itself well worth the sixpence charged for the magazine. There are plenty of other pictures large and small to illustrate the plentiful supply of verse and stories. There is a page -devoted to the awarding of prizes in the 1886 competition, and announcement is made as to special competitions for the year 1887. "The Magazine of Art" for January has for fron- tispiece a highly finished and striking etching of C. H. Broughton's painting of "The Councillors of Peter the , Headstrong.' The charming illustrations or "Round about West Drayton" make one more and more in love with our own country. There are most readable illustrated papers on "Glimpses of artist- life," " The Power of the Revolution,' "A kingly Architect," and" An Artist in Design ' while "The Chronicle of Art" keeps the reader posted up to the end of the year. "The Lady's World," also published by Messrs Cassell, reaches its third number' and is likely to prove a most eucoessful venture. It is afashi on jour- nal, and it is something more; for amongst the contents of the present issue we have Society Gossip, A Christ- mas Comedy, Pastimes for ladies, Dramatic notes. Christmas in the shops, A chat about books, Musical notes, and the art of giving dinners, In " Cassell's National Library" series the latest issue is "A Christmas Carol" and "The. Chimes," by Charles Dickens. "The Season" illustrated lady's magazine is to hand for January, with its coloured plates, Paris fashions, and designs in fancy-work, needle-work, embroidery, &et.

, VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT WARRINGTOIN.

-- The distribution of prizes, presented by local tradesmen, and won in tbe annual Christmas con- tests by the members of the Ist Volunteer Battalion of the South-Lancashire Regiment, late 9th' took place in the Drill Hall, Bath-street, on Thurs- day evening week. The room had been ab. tractively decorated for the recent ball, and these decorations gave the proceedings additional interest. In the Christmas contests there were 122 competitors, and the prizes amounted to 104. Thel chair was occupied by Major Bolton, and he was supported by Captain Ridgeway and Captain Buck- ton. There was a good attendance. After an opening selection by the bend of the regiment, Mims BOLTON spoke of the kindness of the tradesmen of the town in coming forward so handsomely in their contributions towards the Christmas prize fund. He observed that their regi- mental prizes were not en numerous as they might have been, as the local gentry had not given as many subscriptions as other corps received, and they had to fall back upon their own resources. It was grati- fying to see the manner in which the tradesmen of the town had come forward, and they were grate- ful to them. They hoped they would not fail to come forward in a similar manner in future, and they hoped there would be an improvement in trade during next year. (Applause.) Captain RIDGWAY said he thought it was very good on the part of the tradesmen alrarrinron to come forward with their prizes so generous y. As far as he could see they had done very well during the past year, and better, perhaps, than they could be expected. The men had turned up very well at , the drills, and the number who made themselves efficient was found to be larger than on any previ- cue occasion. The Government grant would there- fore be increased, and he trusted it would enable them to do something more next year in the way of drills, or an amendment, if possible. He pointed out they had not yet been able to secure a "camp- ing out" away from Warrington, and said he thought if they were able to have that it would do ! a great deal of good towards increasing their steadiness and setting them up in a better manner ! than the simple battalion drills which they had at present. (Hear, hear.) If the Government would only come forward with an increased capitation grant they might be able to do something in that ' direction 'before long. The Government ought not to put them to such an expense in the way of en- campment as they did at present. He thought there was no reason why permanent camps should not be established in the country for allowing the different battalions to have encampments when it was possible for them to do so. He concluded byl referring to the suggested introduction of the re- peating rifle into the regular army, and said he hoped it would not be long before that was done. (Applause.) Major Bolton and Captain Ridgway then pro- ceeded to distribute the prizes. The following is the list of prize winners -Ist. Bandmaster ARMSTRONG then came forward, and, on behalf of the band, presented to the officers a handsome silver cup, won by the band at the Liver- pool Exhibition on the occasion of their visit at the invitation of Sir David Ratcliffe. He formally asked their acceptance of the cup, which was handed to Major Bolton, who in responding on be- halg of the officers, said it gave him great pleasure to receive it, and on a future occasion the officers would only be too glad to make some suitable re- cognition of their kindness in presenting them with the cup. (Applause.) Major BOLTON, in moving a vote of thanks to the donors of the prizes, said he could not express toe deeply the satisfaction they felt in having the suP- port of the local tradesmen. (Applause.)—Thei motion was carried with cheers. Cordial thanks to the officers for presenting the prizes, and the sergeants who collected the prises, ,eoucluded the proceedings.

FATAL BOXING MATC/L—Dating the festivities at Wool. wish Barracks on Christmas Day, two soldiers, named Lee and Jones, had a boxing match, which turned to a fight. Jones fell, and was picked op dead. The adjutant, on re- , oeiving the report of the occurrence, ordered all dancing to be /topped and the civilians to leave the barracks. lii, stated in Dablin that Mr. William O'Brien has com- menced ait action against the proprietors of the " Dublin Deily Express" for £5,000 damages for an alleged libel in the eorrespondence and leading columns of this journal, in I which the plaintiff is charged with being a swindler and an "Invineible." TER Sar.v.trunt AaxY.--The return of" General" Booth from his tram-Atlantis trip was made the oseasien, on Saturday, of a demonstration by his "army.' Some 4,000 Salvatioalets met him at Easton station, and 'escorted him to Exeter Hall, where he received a public welcome from his followers. Many speeches were made, inspiriting sta- tistics were quoted and there was great rejoicing. BauTAL IttTRDIR cit InsLearsi.—At Dublin, on Tuesday, • ooroner's jury, at an inquest on a woman named O'Brien, found a verdict that the demased died from the effects of al biasing she had re/sired from her husband and mother on Christmas Eve. The Coroner mid that the wise was a Venially brutal one, and that he hoped that the fall penalty of the law would be inflisted on her husband and mother. CARRYING • DRAD CHILD ABOOT.—The police arrested, on Monday, at Kinnitty, King's County, a wandering luna- tic named Troy, who was found eight miles distant from his home in a nude state, and with the dead body of his son, four. Yam old, clasped to his breast. The little one had died from exposure. The poor fellow, about whose demented condition there could be no doubt, became, on being deprived of the corpse, exceedingly violent, and it was with difficulty that he was secured and removed to an asylum. Tan Sam= or CONTIN2NTAL Matzs.—Tbe Belgian Pos- tal Administration is now constructing a model van for the eonveyance of Inglish and Transatlantic mails from Ostend to Herbesthal on the German frontier. Thie van, of the size of a saloon carriage, will be divided int* two compart- ments, one to be used as a travelling post office, and the other for the safe keeping of letters and parcels contain- ing valuables and of registered letters. In the meantime ' provisional measures have been taken to secure the safety of the mails. EXCITING SCINII AT A FlRR.—Early on Saturday morn- ing a fire was discovered at the shop of Mr. Stevens, painter and paperhanger, in Exe Island, Exeter. The firemen were playing non the flames from the roof of a shop adjoin- ing, when the building collapsed, and six or seven men fell into the open space below. Fortunately, the barns and rafters fell in ends a way ac-oss the cavity as to save the men from being crushed to death ; but it was with great difficulty they were rescued. One man had his leg broken, and four or five others were bruised and shaken.

Cutrnisteruaxs.—The British &seociation have published a report of their investigations into the question of cente- narianism. Fifty-two cases of persons attaining the age of 100 years are given. Of these no fewer than 12 had been teetotallers all through life or for a long period, 29 took very little intoxicating drink, and eight were moderate drinkers. Among • living veteran teetotallers mention is made of M. Cbevreul, the French chemist. A fatuous Lon- don abstainer, Dr. Wielobycki, who is 93 years of age,walke twelve miles daily, and is said to be on th e top of Primrose Hill every morning Wore nine-tenths of Londoners have breaktatted.

CANON WILENRFORCS IN A NONOONFORMIST PULPIT.— At the Albion Congregational Chanel, Southampton, on Sunday evening, Canon Wilberforce preached in connection with the monthly special service. No previous announce- ment was made, except among Nonconformists. The canon was introduced by the pastor, the Bev. S. G. Matthews, who said that he was glad to see him there for other reasons than the exhibition of Christian fellowships between churches of different denominatiens.—Catton Wilberforce prayed that God's blessing might rest upon the paster and the Albion Church, also the Church u niversal, and that men might 'reach over barriers to join those engaged in Christian work. He afterwards delivered a powerful gospe I address, but made no further reference to his appearance there. _ • _ . .

TEE CAMPBELL CAsE.—A NEW TRIAt.—.It is stated that a uotice of motion for a now trial of the suit of 'Campbell v. Campbell" was on Friday filed at the Divorce Registry, Solihrset House, by Messrs. C. 0. Humphreys and Sons, solicitors for Lord Colin Campbell. on the ground that the verdict of the jury in the recent trial was against the weight of evidence; also on the ground of 4` misdirection and the absence of a proper and complete direction to the jury upon the law, and as to the efidence applicAble" to the issues, and also upon the ground of the improper admission and rejection Of evidence. The court will be further moved on behalf of Lord Colin Campbell to vary so much of the decree of the judge as condemns Lord Colin Campbell in the coats of the Duke of Marlborough,. naptain Shaw, and Mr. T. Bird. The application will be Made on•the 11th of January, or as soon after as possible.

THE MURDER AT Ansisom.—A magisterial investigation MSS held at Armagh on Monday to inquire into the m nrder of the young man, John Proctor. The prisoners Patrick Gartland and James McKenna were present in custody, and were loudly cheered on their wav to the courthouse. During the proceedings, Mr. Williamson, sMieitor for the prisoners, was several times cautioned by Mr. Hamilton, resident ma- gistrate, who threatened to norarnit him to gaol for contempt of court. Mr. Williamson still persisted in his remarks, and in the end he was committed to gaol. The case was, then adjourned for eight days. On emerging from the court Gartland, who is accused of the murder, was lifted by some of the crowd and chaired. Mr. Williamson was cheered all the way to prison, at the gates of which a number of people remained hooting and cheering for some time. Later on, parties paraded the streets, shouting for Home Rule and cheering Mr. Williamson. As regards the 1 Court-house Itself, RO such Ecene has ever probably oc- I cured there before. TRR Tints or ARGYLL AND HIS CROITTEHS.—The fol- lowing letter -from the Duke of Argyll to his crofter tenants in Tiree,Th replying to a communication from them regard- ing the withholding of arrears until the crofters question is dealt with by the Land Court, has been published in Oban - Incernry„ Jobs Campbell. John M'Kinnanond others, —Until about three years ago I had no reason to•comPlain of any of you, but since that time souls of yds have been taking advantage of lawlessness to avoid paying your lust debts. lam quite willing to allow for bad market during the past year. You are mistaken about the intentions of the Crofters Act. It Was never intended to. encourage tensiate to withhold rents whielr they can pay till the Commission comes. lam going to apply' to the Commission, as well at you, and I am quite willing to leave one-third of your arrears to remain unpaid till the rents are settled by corn- mission; but the amount yen, are withholding; sometimes more than two years' rent, is quite unreasonable. I hope the time will soon return when you' will have pride in discharging year obligatione like other honest men. —• ARGYLL."

GREAT FIRE IN LIVERPOOL —Lutvls's Es-rantisnarmyr Des-rizoyen.—A destructive fire broke out at two o'clock a.m. on Friday, at Lewis's extensive establishment, Liver- pool. The part destroyed is that in which drapery, patent medicines, tin ware, and confectionery were sold, besides which there was in one part a small menagerie. The flames spread with such alarming rapidity that,. before assistance arrived, the upper part of the great clock tower, 200 feet In height, was thorosghly ablaze. At about a quarter to three the immense wall dividing the Lawton-street estahhehment fell with a terrible crash, and the flames then spread in the' direction of Itanelagh-street, the main front of the building. A square tower, 100 feet high, in that portion was-ablaze by half-past two, and the whole of the building was inevitably doomed. It was not until the handsome pile had been gutted that the flames showed any signs of abating. Piaci; Really none of the contents were saved, the animalk ' thtf menagerie being burnt to death. Fortunately the effortVoll' the firemen were successful in prev.enting the flames eprearlcs' ing to the adjoining blocks, but many of the poorer itt• habitants, fearing that their dwellings would also be con- sumed, made preparations for flight, and hastily removed'' their furniture into the open thoroughfare. The total dam- age is estimated at £300,000. On Monday many thousands of persons visited the scene of the great conflagration. Be- I log bank holiday there were many excursionists in the town, and nearly all the visitors made for Ranelagh-street. The walls and the tower of the buildings next the Central station were considered unsafe, and it was deemed wise to attempt te remove them. With this object gunpowder and dynamite were employed. For some time the efforts to destroy the wall and the tower were unavailing; but during the afternoon the desired end was accomplished. The crowd had been kept back to a safe distance, and the work of demolition was carried out without any personal injury. The result of this °potation was to remove the risk of the tower and the damaged portion of the wall unexpectedly falling outwards to the danger of passers-by. It also en-; sblee the architects and others who are engaged for Messrs.' Lewis to commence the work necessary for the restoration of the building. jar ALL Wno USN SurcLaaa's COLD-WATER BOAP should see that they get the REAL ARTICLE—as some unfair shop- keepers, for the sake of extra gala, r eve been detected in palm- ing oft Counterfeits, trading on tiinclair's repute' ion. The second team were the victors by two goals, two tries, and three minors, to a few minor points. Rurrooriri T. Astrrox.—The Aihton-under-Lyne club sent a strong team to Runcorn, on Monday to play off an en- gagement with that local club. There was a large crowd of spectators. and the game proved of an exciting character. The home tears showed well after their spell of idleness, and they won a good game, by a goal, three tries, and half a docen minors to nil. Broady, who played on the wing three-quarter was in grand form. Speakman showed up better than he has done for several weeks while Hughes and Andrews took their full share of work, the latter scoring a try. The forwards were also in good form. WARRINGTON Y. Winar.—The Warrington lads journeyed to Wigan on Obstatmas Day to meet Stavie's combination. The earlier part of the week was very frosty. and on Tues. 1 day night there was very little prospect of a"game taking place, but on Wednesday rain fell, and there was a fair pro- I bability of the match ooming off. The visitors arrived aoont three o'clock, and quickly made tracks for the ground, which was virttrilly a puddle hole, and was grettiv detri- mental to anything like very fast play. Some 12,000 spec• barns had assembled round the ropes to witness the encoun- ter, which proved to he of a very tine open description. At the Glose the game stood Warrington 4 minors, Wigan 5, no major point being scored, From first to last the ball was kept continnally on the more, both lots of forwards playing a grand combined game, whilst the backs—especi- ally Gilbert, Appleton, and Jolley (Warrington), and Ander- ton and Sleyln Wigan)--made the most of their opportu- nities. The first-named on one or two occasions almost ecored, whilst Anderton on one occasion looted like getting over. It would be only fair to add that Warrington was only poorly represented, being without Ashton, Fair Tur- ner, Tommy Barnes, and Hough, whilst Wigan, besides hav- ing their usual team, obtained assistance from Roylance, of Blackrod fame. Had the ground been in better condition the Warrington lads would have shown up much better, as the backs just now are playing a splendid game. WARRINGTON V. MR._ JORDAN'S BROUGHTON

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

- - The great gathering of spectators on the Warrington ground•on Monday received an excellent treat in witness- ing the match between the home team and Broughton. Notwithstanding the good reputation of the latter, and in spite of their really flue play, it is'no more than fair to say that they were about overwhelmed by their opponents, and had it not been for the very unusual kicking powers of their full back they would have been "allied!' At the same time it must be confessed that after Coop bad piloted the leather over the cross bar from about the middle of the field in the superb manner he did it looked rather dark for Warrington so far as points were concerned. But " well that ends well," and this very unexpected stroke of lack for the visitors only resulted in bringing out a little more of the I latent capacity of Gilbert' pack. The Warrington " A " team played a fine and successful game on Saturday, and put in another claim to be con- sidered the premier "A" team for some considerable dis- tance round. It is true their ranks were strengthened by " Tommy " Batmesoeho is a host in himself, but it is not

!likely that the result would have been much diffsrent in any ease. It was rather curious, though, to see bow Barns played with his opponents, who seemed rather helpless in dealing with bitn sometimes.

On Ronda,. Broughton Rangers made a journcy to Bar- row to play off a fixture with the home teams, and the Northerners proved too much for them, the game ending— Barrow, two tries and four minors; Broughton, one try and two minors. In association circles the most notable match was that between Preston North End and Bolton Wanderers In which the wanderers suffered defeat at the bands of their redoubtable opnonenta to the tane of twelve goals to Ohs.

div.head: CHRISTMAS FESTrVITIES AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: CHRISTMAS FESTrVITIES AT EARLESTOWN.

The advent of Christmas at Rariestown and New- ton was heralded by the playing of a brass band, and the peregrinations of a few bands of carol singers. During the morning and forenoon the weather was not of a very encouraging character, showers of rain and hail occasionally falling. The day was observed as a general holiday, all business and work being entirely suspended. The Viaduct Works stopped on the Friday night until next Mon- day, while the Vulcan Iron-foundry stopped on the same day, but resumed work on Monday morning last. The holidays there, however, will be resumed on ' Friday night until the following Thursday morning. There were few public attractions, locally, on Christmas Day. The local political clubs were well patronised by the members. At one or two places of worship special services were held, and treats to poor children took place at the Bruns- wick Wesleyan School, Cross-lane, and the Congre- gational School, Crow-lane. The annual Sunday school tea party was held in the Primitive Metho- dist School-room, Legh-street. An announced foot- ball match between the Earlestown Club and Bolton Temperance Club did not take place owing to the failure of the visitors to put in an appearance. Re- ports of gatherings are appended. TREAT TO RAGGED SCHOOL CHILDREN. At the invitation of Mr. B. B. Glover, of Crow-lane, the scholars who habitually atteod the Ragged School, in Lech- street, Barlestown were entertained to a substantial din- ner of meat, potatoes, and plum pudding, at noon, on Christmas Day. Toth e numberof about 100, the scholars, along with their teachers, met about half-past eleven in the forenoon,' and walked to Crow-lane Congregational Sehoolroom. They were headed by the Superintendent,Mr. J. H. Graham and the • teachers, Mr. James Woods, Mr. Thomas Martindale, Mr. Pendrey, Mrs. Lovell, and Mrs. Birks. When they arrivea at the school, they found that Its interior had been transformed Into a dining room, the tables pleasantly dmorated with plants and flowers from Mr. Glover's conservatory, (oanaing many a little heart to throb in anticipation of a happy Christmas dinner. The juveniles were qeickly seated, and everyone seemed to thor• oughly enjoy the repast'provided for them. The catering ' for their wante was left in the hands of Mr. H. J. Pond, of ' the Pied Bull Hotel,Newton, and in addition to his waiters the following ladies and gentlemen also attended to the wants of the little ones : Mrs. Allatt, the Misses Allatt (two), the Mimes Glover (two), Mrs. Birks, Mrs. Thomas Martindale, me Woods, Mr. Ming, the local missioner, Mr. Jones, Mr. Alfred Howard, Mr. Sephton, and others. Imme- diately after dinner the children sang a hymn entitled "Jesus, keep me near the cross," and an entertainment fol- lowed. The Rev. James Allan addressed a few words to the children, in the course of which be referred to the good results that had followed the work of the Bagged School, and observed as they celebrated Christ's birthday on Christmas Day, that gathering was really a birthday party. Addresses appropriate to the oc- casion were also given by Mr. Dring and Mr. Woods. The Congregational IChapel choir rendered a few selec- tions under the• leadership of Mr. A. Caldwell, the organist, and solos were sang by Miss Anat. Mr. A. Caldwell, and Mr. John Caldwell. The Rev. J. Allatt asked the children to give three cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Allatt for their kindness, a requeet which was warmly responded to.—Mr. Glover acknowledged the compliment, and said he hoped that if they did not next year obtain a similar dinner at his invitation sonrorm would follow the I example that had that del been set. The children after- wards enioyed themselves in a field near Mr. Glover's house The proceedings from beginaing to end were heartly enjoyed by the little children, and It was felt on every hand that the generosity of Mr. and Mrs. Glover was well worthy of commendation, and it is to be hoped that the custom thus commenced will not be allowed to lapse for the lack of followers of Mr. and Mrs. Glover's example. BAND OF KINDNESS TREAT TO POOR CHILDREN.

Under the ausbices Earle" branch of the Band of Kindness, an institution for securing from young folks, a pledge of kindness to all domestic animals and birds, a gathering of an exemplary character, was held in the Bruns- wick Wesleyan Sunday School, Cross-lane, Earlestown, on Christmas morning. This consisted of a free breakfast of a substantial character to over 300 of the poorest of chil- dren resident in the neighbourhood. The cost of this break- fast was defrayed by subscriptions collected from local gen- tlemen and hulk% among those who libchtily centrlbuted being Mrs. Evans (Elaydock), Colonel George McCorqdee dale, J.P., Mr. A. C, McCorquodale. J.P., Mr. T. J. Gillen- pie, J.P., Mr. W. F. Gooch, J.P., Mews. T. Molynettx, R. H. Wright, T. Stone, C. B. F. Broom, ire. Theltrrangements for the gathering were made by the following committee of workers of the local bratich of the Band of Kinduess : Mr. Thomas Roberts (presiding officer), Mr. H. Taylor (secre- tary), Mr. H. Jackson (registrar), Miss Needham (trea- surer), Misses Clare. Edith Jackson, Newman, and Alderson (two), and Messrs. J. Parr and Joseph Birchall. To this energetic and hardworking committee the thanks of the children are dun for the enjoyable breakfast to which they were treated. irrespective of the religious persuasions of parents all poor children were invited to the feast, and to each clergyman and minister a number of tickets for distri- bution among the most deserving cases coming under their notice, were forwarded. In every case, with one exception, these tickets were accepted, and the children-recipients anxiously awaited the advent of Christmas. At nine o'clock on the morning of that day over 300 children met at the Wesleyan School, as stated, and Were quickly provided with seats at the attractive tables. Each " guest " was presented with a bag, which contained a pork pie, a mince pie, a scone, and a piece of currant bread, while they were regaled with an ample supply of tea, served. In addi- tion to this, each of the children, On leaving the room, WAS given another bag, in which was an orange, an apple, and a meat pie. Breakfast being over an enjoyable entertainment followed. Miss Bothwell nicely sang "He wipes the tear from every eye ; " Mr. C. Corlett gave "Be kind," aed the Pianoforte and vocal selection," Chime egain,bearittfni bell," by the Misses Allatt, was highly appreciated. The harMo• nium accompaniments of Mr. B. Corlett were finely rendered. Daring the morning a few words to the children were spoken by Mr. Dring, the town missionary, and the Rev. Robert Carr (Primitive Methodist), and Mr. B. B. Glover. A cordial and deserving vote of thanks was passed to the committee of the Band of Kindness for their exertions in providing the free breakfast, to which Mr. T. Roberts, Presiding Officer, replied. The entertainers and lowl gen- tlemen present partook of a light luncheon during the proceedinra. PRIMITIVE METHODIST TEL PARTY.

- _ The annual tea party in connection with the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, Legh-etreet, Earleetown, was held in the new school-room, Lord-street, on the afternoon of Christmas Day. The room had been attractively decorated with evergreens, mottoes, &0., under the direc- tions of Messrs. T. Travis, Pendrey. Sirett, J. Sproston, Taylor, Auetin, T. Hankey, J. Sankey, J. Worslev, About 100 persons sat down to an excellent tea, aftsr which a miscellaneous entertainment was given. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Robert Carr, resident member, who, in the course of an address commenting on a dialogue in which it was etated that charitable institutions were the glory of England, said it spoke well for England that she provided so many charitable institutions, but it was a shame that so many institutions were needed, and they should devote their attention to the cauees of such pauperism, poverty, and crime. During the evening Arthur Arrow- smith recited "An opening address," Rachel Thompson recited "The beggarman," Charles Dickens recited Christ- mas Eve," Sarah Jane Johnston gave "The widow's wealth," a dialog-ne. "What can wc do?" was given by Annie Woreley, ME. Whittaker, H. Line, end S. A. Barton ; John Peadrey recited "Keep your reco-d clean," J Banton re- cited "Keep at it," J W Austin gave "The Christian hero," E Worsley recited " The doctor's story,"‘a dialogue, entitled "The waggling tongue," was given by J Sephton, E Dickens, A and M Massey, S J Woods, and S J Arrowsmith ; recitation, "A father te his motherless children," N Peers: recitation, " A merry Christmas," Richard Stevens; recita- tion, "The child's first grief," J Crosby; recitation, "Bruce and the spider," Nally Thompson; recitation, "The little , orator," G S Surgees; trio, "The little farm," J Huddles- tono J Austin, and J Banton; dialogue, "Sabbaths mis- spent,' T Travis, J Worslev, J Woods, and B Worsley ; reci- tation, "Forgiving Jenny," M E Mills; recitation. "Waiting for a footstep that we know," E J Stevens; recitation," The angel at the gate," DI Harrison; recitation, "Boys' and girls rights," E Goodwin; dialogue, "Five clever men of Ruetown,7 3 Sankey, J Hall, W Arrowsmith. A ad B Sephtom, and T. Mulkey. The various items were highly appreciated:.

!I leader of the House of Commons to a policy which he cannot defend. It may be that in resigning Lord RANDOLPH is acting on some understanding with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. It has been obvious all along that he could not count on the support of the member for Bir- mingham and other Radical Unionists, if the County Government Bill was of a reactionary kind; and, failing that support, the life of the Government would not be worth a month's purchase. What is it worth vow? —that has become the question of the hour. If Lord SALISBURY cannot shape his proposed legislation in a spirit sufficiently Liberal to satisfy a professed Tory like the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, how is it to be expected that it will give satisfaction to professed Liberals like Lord HARTINGTON ? And with- out the support of the Liberal Unionists the Government mu,t cease to exist. Lord HAR- TINGTON is altogether too shrewd and too cautious to rush in where a CHURCH- ILL fears to tread. As to a Coalition Govern- ment, that is a thing which is made not to work, but to go to pieces. The probability therefore is that we shall have another General Election before many more months have passed. Let us hope that it will not come until the Liberals are so united as to be Able to carry the country with a rush, and thus ensure a good working majority.

THE watchmakers of Prescot are suffering, and have suffered for some time, through a falling off of trade. They complain strongly that they are feeling the ill effects of fraudu- lent practices on the part of Swiss watc;i manufacturers. It is alleged, and the state- ment does not appear to be disputed, that the ' Swiss makers are in the habit of putting in- ferior movements into English hall-marked cases, and then selling them as English watches. The difficulty seems to be that, as the law stands, there is no means of putting a stop to the practice. If the cases presented for marking are found to be of standard qual- ity they are marked as such, irrespective of what is done with them. Sir JOHN BENNETT, who is regarded as an authority in the watch trade, contends that the English are left behind because they cannot compete with the Swiss in the open market ; but, lif this be so, it is pertinent to ask, as was asked at the public meeting in Prescot, on Wednesday, how it hap- pens that the foreign maker takes the the trouble to put his movements in Eng- lish cases? It is evident that the manufac- turers of these cheap watches are trading on a reputation which is not their own: and this, to say the least of it, is not legitimate trading. Whether the legislature can inter- fere with advantage to protect the home trade and the home customer is regarded as doubt, . . Tully the authoritie§ who have thus fat been interviewed. "Protection" pure and simple is out of the question; but it remains to be seen whether the law cannot be altered so as to put a stop to something which looks very much like fraud. We punish people for adulteration, and for obtaining money under false pretences; and it seems to us to smack of both offences to palm a watch off as an English watch when there is nothing Eng- lish about it but the case. The question is , certainly one that requires to be fully inves- tigated; and we trust that the Prescot Watch Trade Association will obtain the sympathy and support of the public in pressing their demands upon the attention of Parliament.

WARRINGTON has this week lost one of her most distinguished sons by the death of Mr. JOHN WARRINGTON WOOD; and that the loss was widely felt was made evident by the numerous and touching references to his memory which have been heard on every hand. He was a true son of the people; he was known as a youth and young man as a mason's apprentice, and it is, in part, on that account that his death has made so strong an impression on the popular mind. This im- pression has been heightened, too, by the circumstances of his death. He had left his native town to reside at Rome, the home of the sculptor, and had come back in the plen- itude of his power, and with fame attending him, to execute various commissions of his townsmen. One only of these was completed when he was seized with the illness which proved fatal in a few days. It is noted as singularly suggestive of the mutability of human affairs that but a few weeks ago Mr. WOOD had to relinquish the work of modelling a bust of the MAYOR because of that gentleman's sudden and alarming ill- ness; and that, while his Worship still lies prostrate on a bed of sickness, the sculptor is himself struck down and carried to the I grave. It is something to reflect that Mr. WARRINGTON WOOD has not passed away as one who will be heard of no more. He leaves a record in his work of which future generations may be proud, while his name I will be an incentive to other sons of toil to make the best of the talents with which they have been endowed. It is to the credit of the town that by providing a School of Art so many years ago, it gave genius the op- portunity of ascertaining and developing its powers. The sculptor who passed to his rest on Sunday was not less a credit to the School; and we need hardly add that War- rington will in future be known and honoured as the birthplace of WARRINGTON WOOD.
"TOUCH AND GO." Reader, "A Happy New Year to you." There's a new foot on the floor, my friend, And a new face at the door, my friend, A new face at the door.

Two football players have been badly hurt, at St. Helens—one on Christmas Day and the other on Monday last. It is the spice of dan- ger, of course, which makes the game re- lished ; but when a'player gets his leg bro- ken he probably thinks he has more than his share of the spice.

What with the intense cold, and the dense fog, the weather on Thursday was murderous. Several persons have lost their lives—two in Liverpool, two at Stalybridge, and one at Runcorn. Edward Guest was the name of the young man who was drowned at Runcorn. He missed his footing in the dark and slipped into the dock. A splash and a plunge and all was o'er, And the waves rolled on as they rolled. before.

Bromby, the clergyman who officiates there. It is nothing more nor less than a surplice for the ladies in the choir. who supplement the singing of the men and boys. The ladies take to it of course. When were they knovn to object to putting on a new dress?

They deserve all they get in this way, for competition is keen, and efficiency is not attained without the sacrifice of a great many leisure hews. , eeing that they get such excellent service Ifrom our Volunteers, the Government would I do well to spend a little more money on them year by year. If they want to retrench, let them strike at the Pension List.

The Earlestown magistrates have fined a boy one shilling and costs for snowballing passers-by. Lads should be made to under- stand that snowballing can only be tolerated when it is confined to themselves. It is "greit fun," but it is fun of a cowardly kind when half-a dozen youths take to pelting a defenceless. girl or woman. Cases of this kind call for the intervention of the police- man. Boys who cannot learn good be- haviour otherwise must have a lesson in the police court.

"Pity the sorrows of a poor Prime Minis- ter" is the new version of an old song which Lord Salisbury is called upon to sing. Lord Randolph has left him, and as to Lord Hartington, although he .comes all the way from Rome at his entreaty, he will not enter a Cabinet with him. Why does not the Prime Minister wake up the dormant To!), talent of which we have heard so much ? Or why not take in Mr. Goschen ? The Liberals can spare Mr. Goschen ; they have been taken in by him often enough.

The new lifeboat for Southport was tested on Wednesday, at Southport, in the presence of a large number of persons. On being cap- sized, even with mast and sails set, she promptly self-righted, thereby fully restoring confidence in the self-righting principle at Southport. As nothing succeeds liko, success, the boat has been fitted with all the latest improvements of the Lytham Lifeboat, which saved the crew of the Mexico. After the terrible catastrophe the other week, the Life. boat Institution should have all the older life- boats thoroughly overhauled,

The military man with a craze would im- poverish the country to defend it until there was nothing left to defend. General Bou- langer, the French Minister of War, originally asked for a credit of three hundred millions of francs, but now he can, it is stated, see his way to getting along with forty-three millions. He would, of course, have spent the big sum, if he could have had it. " It's a mad world, my masters," and will be so long as "monarchs and statesman " are allowed to set people at each other's throats who ought to meet each other as brothers.

The re-issue of }hinds History of Lanca- shire brings under notice the fact that by royal proclamation in 1314 the price of "the best cow alive and fat" was to be izs ; "the best goose 3d," and "20 eggs id." These were maximum prices, and existed for twelve years. What if Her Majesty were to issue a similar royal proclamation to hold good not for twelve years, but for twelve days during the Jubilee Year? A goose for 3d.—think of it you who have seen and smelled, but not tasted, the bird this Christmas. And "zo eggs id"—why the boys could play mar- bles with them all day, and grow fat on the game.

In the new number of "The Nineteenth Century," Mr. Gladstone reviews the old and new poems of " Locksley Hall "—or rather the history of the periods out of which they have been evolved. Whatever certain critics may think as to signs of weakness in the poet laureate, no one who reads this article will venture to suggest that the ex- Premier's natural force has abated; and most people will agree with him, when he says— " The country is still young as well as old, and in these latest days it has not bee.a un- worthy of itself. Justice does not require, nay rather she forbids, that the Jubilee of the Queen be marred with tragic tones."

The authorities of the Lancashire County Constabulary have hit on a happy thought in giving special ° encouragement to constables to make themselves proficient members of the "St. John Ambulance Association." Who so likely as a policemen to render first aid, when he knows how, to an injured per- son? Out of about 72 members of the St. Helens force no less than 56 have taken the matter up, and a large number are now recognised as qualified members. As things go, "common bobby" will come to mean the policeman who is not entitled to wear the white silk Maltese cross of the Ambulance Association.

WIDNES Rattan Commirrnn.—For the• purpose of hear- ing application for relief, andmaking the necessary grants in Widnes and the surrounding townships, a Relief Com- mittee has been formed by the Prescot Board of Guardians. The committee consists of the Guardians of Widnes, Cron- ton, Dutton, Halewood, Hale, Speke, and Bold; and its sit- tings will be a great convenience to persons who are com- pelled to seek the aid of poor law administration. . Subs,quently the proceedings took the Character of a ball, a most enjoy- able time being spent in dancing. Mr. F. Joule officiated as MC., and the atewards were Messrs. J. Little, F. Was given by the members and. friends of the club, in the schoolroom, which was kindly lent by the vicar for the occasion. Miss Weier, Messrs. A large and enthusiastic audience I filled the room, and from the hearty and frequent bursts of ,applause, it was evident the concert was enjoyed by all.

Runcoette TONIC-Sore-Re Catorn.—The members of this choir gave a cancert in Runcorn Public Hill. on Tuesdsy evening. There was a moderate attendance. The first part of the p..ogramine consisted of the cantata "Ancient Mariner,' and the chorus, about 30 in number, acquitted themselves very creditably to the directions of Mr. John Holford, the conductor. The second part was composed of miscellaneous items rendered by the incipds—Miss Alice Mouledate. Madam Janet Grieve, Mr. J. T. Sydney, and Mr. P. Richardson. An orchestral band, under the control at Mr. P. Caldwell, junr., of Warrington, rendered good service.

WIDNE3 Rama Vormarramts.—Last night week the an- nual distribution of prizes in connection with the Widnes corps of the 2Lst Lancashire Regiment took place in Or; Volunteer Hall. Seventy volunteers had the honour of re- ceiving prizes for their skill in shooting at the range, and Captain Brunner, in making the presentation, referred to the increased capitation grant which was about to be granted by Government. greater efficiency, he said, would be requires}, from the volunteers for this iocrease in the money devoted to the purposes of voluntary defence, and he expressed the hope that the Widnes volunteers would make a perceptible ad VACS.

FUNERAL AT RuNcoaN.—Yesterday week the remains of Miss Fanny Cook, the daughter of Mr. Thomas Cook, boot manufacturer, Church-street, were interred at the Runcorn Cemetery amid many signs of sorrowing. The deceased, who was a young lady of 24 years of age, bad been brought up under the influences of Camden Sunday School, and was a regular attendant at St. Paul's Chapel; and a number of prominent members of the latter place of worship paid the last respects to the dead. The hearse was followed by the 1 father and two brothers of the deceased, and a number of relatives, while it was preceded by the Rev. A. P. Watson, who officiated at the grave, Messrs. Robert Norman, J. Ra- ley, 13. Coventry, I. Bowyer, G. Yarwood, W. Croley, Spearing,Molyneux, Massey, Collins, Byrne, T. Foster, F. Bibby, T. Lea, T. Crosby, J. W. Woodland, T. Furneval, &c. The deceased, who suffered a long illness, is deeply regretted by a large number of friends. Ruttcoais PARISA Ceufeca.—The commencement of the year will see great activity in connection with the Parish Church of Runcorn. This (Saturday) morning, at eleven o'clock, Holy Communion will lie celebrated by the Lord 'Bishop of the Diocese. In the afternoon the recently ap- pointed Vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A., will be in- stituted into his living. The ancient ceremony will be per. formed by the Bishop of Chester, who will preach a sermon. Afterwards the service of Induction will be performed by the Archdeacon. It is expected that the Vicar will preach his first sermon on Sunday evening, On the following Thursday the parishioners will give the Vicar a hearty welcome to the town. The proceedings are to take the form of a congregational tea party on a more elaborate scale than usual. Subsequently a concert, for which a most attractive programme has been arranged, will be Riven, and speeches by tha Vicar and others will form an interesting item at this period of the history of the Run- corn Church.

SMITA 9 ALMANAC AND DIRIECTOMY.—The Almanac ar.d Directory arranged by Messrs. P. Smith St Co., chemists and druggists, Runcorn, has just been published, and is a monu. trent to the enterprise and energy of the proprietors. The publicitions of the past eight years are totally eclipsed by the volume for 1887. Besides the usual information of an almanac, there is considerable literary matter of an enter- taining an 4 instructive character, and a number of pages are devoted to an excellent guide to household management. The chief and most important feature of the book, which contains 600 pages, is the directory of the twin towns of the Mersey—Runcorn and Widnes—and the surrounding vil- lages of Frodsham, Halton, Norton, Astimoor, Daresbury, Moore, Stockbam, Preston Brook, Sutton, on the Cheshire aide, and Appleton, Farnworth, Bold, ctc., on the Lancashire side. It is customary to include in a directory only the names of the chief res Pents and the places of business, but Messrs. Smith have gore much beyond this limit. Each ratepayer and householder in the districts covered find a place in the directory', which is printed in good clear 'type, and is admirably arranged for reference. The book deserves a large circulation, and we believe will become a necessity of every household library.

CHRISTMASTIDE AT Rmecranx.--Christrnas was celebrated in the customary manner at Runcorn. Although the weather was very cold and damp, rain frequently falling, yet the last stroke of twelve bad scarcely struck before the carol singers were making the air melodious with their hymns of praise. Not so pleasant were the vocal outpourings of gangs of lads, who, though young In years, were men in their own estimation ; and it is to be regretted that some limit was not put to their perigrinations. Sunshine brightosed Christmas morning, but in the afternoon dark clouds hid the sky. and at night there was a heavy fall of rain and sleet. At the churches of the Establishment special services were held during the day, and were fairly well attended. The Parish Church had been tastefully and appropriately decorated, and presented a pleasant appear- ance. There were no amusements provided in the tewn, but many made merry with their friends' and hundreds travelled to Liverpool in search of pleasure. The poor were not for- gotten. It cannot ba said that there Is mach distress in the town, but there are members of poor families ever in need of the hand of charity, and Mr. Charles Wigg generously provided a substantial repast for 110 such cases. To the order of Mr. Wigg, Mr. Robert Gorst, confectioner, High. street, prepared 110 hot-pots, each dish containing upwards of fillns. of potatoes and beef. The various clergymen and ministers were entrusted with the distribution of the tickets amongst the needy, and between twelve and one o'clock Mr. Gorst's premises presented a bustling appearance. Gratitude was depicted upon the faces of the recipients of Mr. Wigg's generosity as they bore away the steaming dishes.

CEIRISTMASTIDS AT Wrprrits.—The almost ceaselesa ac- tivity of the chemical centre had a brief period of quietude at Christmas. The great religious festival was observed on all hands by a holiday spent as the sweet wills of the people direc'ed. The day was heralded in the customary fashion. Mass was said by crowded congregations at the Catholic Chapels on Christmas Eve, and the choirs of the different churches and Nonconformist Chapels sung carols at the residences of a number of their supporters. On Christmas Day well-attended services were held at St. Mary's and St. Paul's Churches, and at other places of worship in the neighbourhood, all of which were deco, ated to some extent. Many pleasure seekers departed for Liverpool and Manches- ter during the day, but the bulk ef the population stayed at home to make merry. Although work is not scarce in Wid- nes tte poverty-stricken are numerous, and it is pleasing to record that they were not neglected. At the school of the United Methodist Free Church, 150 children of all sizes and all creeds were regaled with A most substantial lareakNat served by the willing hands of the ladies of the congrega- tion. several tradesmen in the vicinity of the school had contributed ham, beef, and tongue, and the repast of which the youngsters so heartily partook was a most excellent one. At dinner tintte 200 children, about whose necessitious cir- cumstances there was not a doubt, were provided with a dinner of potatoe pie and plum pudding in the infants' room of the Simms Cross Board School. The expenditure was borne by the "Free Dinner Fund," inaugurated last win- ter, and in which Mr. S. B. Stringer has taken so warm and active an interest. The subscriptions already received are very encouraging, and it is intended to carry on the RUM. meat during the present winter. The youngsters on Christ- mas Day gave three hearty cheers for their kind patrons before they separated. A CHRISTMAS PRES/MT.—Fifty choice Cigars, in box, post free, for 7s.—J. G. Smoxmcr, Tobacconist, 19,4, Sankey- street, Warrington.—ldef.
