JOHN NIINNEBLEY & CO.—A change, as will be seen from our advertising columns, has been made in the title of this long-established and well-known company. It will be styled in future "The War- rington Slate Company (Limited)," but the business will be carried on precisely as before. The change has been made consequent upon the termination of the seven years for which, it was stipulated, Mr. Nunnerley's name should be used after the business had been converted into the Limited Company which has been managed so successfully. FOOTBALL ACCIDENTS AT Sr. HELENS.—On Christmas Day, during the course of a football match on the St. Helens Recreation ground, one of . _

players named Pilkington was so injured that he had to be carried off the field, and sent home in a cab. On Monday another match was played be- tween the Recreation and a Crewe team, when Peter Proudfoot had his leg broken, and was carried off the field on a stretcher, a great crowd following. LANCASHIRE SESSIONS.—The county justices sit- ting in annual session, on Thursday, at Preston, under the chairmanship of Lord Derby, sanctioned the treasurer's estimates of funds required for county administration to August next. The total amount was £108,600, which was explained to be about the average of the aeast few years. Attention was drawn to the " clashing " of assize and sessions fixtures—,a matter which led to the last Manchester Assizes to some strong remarks by Mr. Justice Cave. In Lancashire there are 56 sessions held each year, for county divisions and boroughs, and it was said to be impossible that assizes should be held without clashing with some of these sessions. It was agreed to send a deputation to the Home Secretary to urge some alteration in the wording of the judges' com- missions, under which in recent years their lord- ships have felt bound to "clear the gaols" of all prisoners awaiting- trial, whether at sessions or assizes. DROWNED AT iturreonx.—A dense fog hung over. Runcorn and neighbourhood all day on Thursday. In the evening, about seven o'clock, it was impossi- ble to see more than three or four yards a head. At this time Edward Guest, 20 years of age, a nattve of Connah's Quay, and mate on board the schooner Miriam Gertrude, of Chester, was walking along side of the Arnold Dock, on the Weston Canal, when he fell into the water. A seaman on board the vessel, named Massey, who had endeavoured to per- suade Guest not to leave the yessel, heard a splash in the water, and a voice call "Tom, Tom, I am in the dock." Owing to the impenetratable fog, no assistance could be rendered to the unfortunate man, whose dead body was recovered on Friday morning and taken to the mortuary. In the after- noon, Mr. J. E. Worsley held an inquest at the Cemetery Office. The jury remarked upon the dangerous nature of the spot where Guest lost his life, and mede a recommendation that tLe side of _ _ _ _
the dock should be protected with a line of chains. The Coroner promised to write to Mr. Meadowcroft on the subject. A verdict of "Accidental death"

was returned. A RUNCORN WOMAN CHARGED WITH CH/LD Dz- sHaTioN.---A woman, who gave the name of Jane Jones, but whose real name is Tudor. the wife of James Tudor, of Greenway-road, Runcorn, was brought before the borough magistrates at War- rington, on Tuesday, charged with neglecting her child by leaving it chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union on the 28th of May last. Evidence was given by Mr. Shearer, relieving officer, to the effect that the child was left by the prisoner, who gave the name of Jones, at a house of a woman named Birehall. Prisoner promised to call again, and to pay a weekly allowance towards the maintenance of the child. She represented that she had come from the South of England. As she did not return the child was taken to the Work- house, where, when nine months old, it died. In- quiries having been made in regard to the matter, the police at Runcorn were communicated with, and the prisoner was apprehended. At first she denied that she was the mother of the child, but the !roman with whom it had been left identified her.

A 'brother of the prisoner, ; dressed was present in court„ and said that his sister had been deserted by her husband, who, he thought. should be made amenable, as he had left his wife with two children. The case was with- drawn onthe brother promising to pay the costs. PRESENTATION TO THE REV. R. EDWARDS, RUNCORN. In the Newtown Mission Room, Shaw-street, Runcorn, Ota Saturday night week, the Rev. R. Edwards, who has accepted the curacy of Childwall, near Liverpool. was presented with an illuminated addrees and a valuable secretaire, in recogni- tion of his labours in the parish of Runcorn during the past four years. Mr. George Surnmerfield presided over the gathering, which was of considerable proportions, and in opening too proceedings, expressed the sorrow felt by the people of Newtown at Mr. Edwards' departure from their midst. Mr, Edwards would leave behind him a deep seuele of his kind acts, and words, and of his faithful work amongst them, and hie memery would remain green in their hearts for many years to come. (Applause.) Mr. C. Pow- nail then read the ald res., as foll.ws:—" Newtewn Mission Church, Runcorn. To the Rev. Robert Edwards, senior curate of the Parish Church, and curate In charge of this Mission. We, the members of the congregation of Newtown Mission Church, and friends in Runcorn and neighbourhood, ask your acceptance of the accompanying Secretaire. They desire to express their high appreciation of the spirit in which you have laboured in the Newtown Mission district and the Parish of Runcorn generally for five yoars, and feel sure that your faithful labeurs will be remembered in after years by many who have been benefitted bv them. They trust you will be spared to see many years of earnest Christian work, and assure you of the sincere and hearty sympatby and love of your friends in Runcorn,—(Signed) George Surnmerfield and Robert Wilson, wardens of New- town Mission Church." The names of the subscribers were appended to the ad- dress. Mr. Pownall remarked that he had worked cordially with

Mr. Edwards for many years, and whenever any money had I been required in connection with the mission Mr. Edwards had always been the first to start the subscription list with a substantial sum. Mr E4wards had taken a deep interest in the work of the parish, and if there had been nothing else he had done, the establishment by him of the Parish Maga- line, which supplied them with valuable information, en- titled Mr. Edwards to their esteem. (Applause.)—Mrs. Whittaker then, on behalf of the subscribers, handed the address to Mr. Edwards.—The secretaire was presented by Mr. Robert Wilaon, who in doing so made a few appro. priate remarks.—The Rev. R. Edwarde, who was cordially received, in acknawledging the presents, said they gave him all the more pleasure because they came trom the members of that part of the parish in which he had done least work, and he thanked them most heartily and sincerely for that expression of their esteem.—On the proposition of Dr. Mac- Dougall, who testified to the value of the labours of Mr. Edwards, a vote ef thanks was accorded to the Chairman and the meeting terminated.—On hunciay morning the rev. gentleman preached his valedictory• sermon at the Parish Church from the words "And new bekold [know, that ye all among whom I have gone preaching shall see my face no more." Alluding to his miniatrations in Runcorn, Mr. Edwards said hia feelings would be unspeakably painful were he not conviaced that in spite of his many deficiencies of which he had been ever sensible, he bad never wilfully kept back any part of the Gospel of Christ. And in the midst of that heaviness of heart which overclouded the I parting hour, he felt joy in the assurance that he had not altogether laboured in vain, nor spent his strength for I nought. He believed, with gladness, that they parted , I with mutual regret, and :though separated from each other, I be should often call to mind the happy hours he had spent I within the border, of that happy parish, and more especially i with him whose call to his well-earned rest necessitated his (Mr. Edwards's) removal from amongst them.
PRESENTATION TO THE REV. T. M. ARMSON, AT RUNCORN. _ _

, The Rev. T. M. Armson, having to vacate his curacy at I.litincorn Parish Church in consequence of the death of the Rev. Canon Barclay. the parishioners determined to show their regard and esteem for the reverend gentleman in a stlbstantial form. AccoiMingly a number of the parishioners , gathered in the National School, on Tuesday evening. to I take part in the presentation to Mr. Armson. Tire gift consisted of Canon Farrar's "Life of Christ "in two vol- umes, and "Eternal hope," by the same author, with a purse containing 25 guineas. The books were inscribed as follows :—'• Presented to the Rev. llamas Manton Armson by the parishioners of Runcorn, together with a purse of gold, as a mark of respect obtained during his six year's' ministry as curate at the Parish Church of All Saints. (Signed) F. A.lLake, William Whittaker,:churchwardens,St. John the Evangelist's Day, DecemLer 27th, 1880." The gold had ben contributed by 90 subscribers. Mr. F. A. Lake presided, and amongst those present were the Rev. I'. M. Armson, Mrs. Lake, Mrs. Whittaker, Mrs. Moss, Mrs. Shaw, Mrs. Sutton, Mrs. Rogerson, Mrs. Kay, Mrs. Hulmes. Messrs. E. Imision, J. N. Zello, J. E. Meredith, W. Mellor, J. Johnson, Jas. Davies, W. Shaw (seamen's missionary), W. Sutton, G. Hewitt, G. Moss, H. Gregory, R. Hulmes, Kay, J. Yates, Cropper, and W. H. Rogerson. The Chairman said they were met together that ev ning, to perform a duty which, to some extent, combined pain and pleasure—the pain which must necessarily be caused by the separation of a clergyman and his dock, and the pleasure that they bad in testifying in some degree to the kindly feelings and good wishes they entertained towards Mr. Armson. (Hear, hear.) Daring the six years that Mr. Armson had held the curacy et Runcorn be bad made no enemies and many friends. (Hear, bear.) As church- warden during the last two years, he (Mr. Lake) had come In constant intercoums with Mr. Armson, and his earnest- ness and patience, kindly disposition, and conciliatory man- ner had, he could assure him, not passed unnoticed; and these qualities had had a very salutory effect upon those with whom he had had to work. (Applause.) Then Mr. Armson's work had not began and ended simply in Church ceremonial, or confined to bis own particular church. There had been nose of the narrow-minded bigotry about Mr. ArtneOn which would prevent him acknowledging that the clergy of other denominations were also working in Christ's vineyard, and that it was quite possible for a Church 'clergyman to work with them to some extent. He had had that true Catholicity which to his mind was the very essence of Christianity. (Applause.) At the Young Men's Christian Associatim Mr. Armson had been found working hand in hand with the clergymen of other denorninatioss, and earning their sincere respect. That his character had not failed to be appreciated the ready way in which so many people had contributed to the testimonial proved. In conclusion the Chairman, on behalf of the par- ishioners, wished him during his future years all those blessings and happiness which the father of all could pos- sibly bestow. (Applause.) Mrs Lake then made the presentation. The Rev. T. M. Armson, in replying,said he could not express all he ought in acknowledging those gifts. Apart from a few hints he received a week ago, that remarkable demonstration of appreciation for part services was totally unexpected, and he should not have blamed anyone in the parish had it not been made, because he could not but know his own capabilities and his own feelings better than anyone else. Although he had had to contend against un- usual obstacles in his work, he had not risen in spite of those obstacles as be ought to have done. Their kind- ness that night weuld give him encouragement in future such as be could not otherwise have had—(bear, hear)— it would enable him to go forth and labour with confidence in the Lords Vineyard its the future, and he ttueted with more earnestness and with a more single eye to God's glory. (Applause) He hoped that in the future God's work would prosper amongst them in a greater de- gree than it had in the past, and that thry would aid their late revered vicar's successor in the good work. He wished to each one present a blessed new year, and prosperity throughout their worldly course, and might they so live that when they came to the final scene, it might be to enter into the joy of the Lord. (Applause.) Mr. W. Shaw spoke of Mr. Armson's earnest lat.saurs, and his readiness to aid in any good canes.

The Chairman remarked' that the thanks of all of them were due to Mr. Mellor and Mr. Sutton for the active in- terest they had taken in getting up that testimonial. Mr. Mellor said that instead of being a labour it had been a very great pleasure indeed both to Mr. Sutton and himself to take the part they bad done. . Mr J. N. Lsllo testified to the pleasure and good he bad received under Mr. Armenia's ministrations.
A vote of thanks having been accorded to the chairman and Mrs. Lake, the meeting, which had been of a most pleasant description, terminated.

Absint 60 members and visitors from other lodges in the district sat down to an excellent dinner served in the lodge room at the London and North-Western Hotel, Lowlands-road. It was the duty of etch member to see that there was nothing dishonest, and, without acting the spy, to see that no man was earning by the sweat of his brow what wv keeping another man in idleness. (Applause.) The Lily of the Valley stood first in the front rank of lodges, and be could not speak too highly of its members or the enterprise that had ever been made to sustain the lodge. He pointed out that the weak spot in these friendly societies was that there was no pension fund out of which members, when de- clared by two medical men to be unable any longer to earn

He was gratified to hear that there was a movement amongst the higher at. tenement of the Order of Oddfellows iii esiab:ish such a pension fund. (Hear, hear.) In handing the clock to Mr. Gleave, Dr. MacDouall expressed the hope that the recipient might be spared many years to look at that timepiece and remember the feelings that had called it forth ; and be trusted to , labour with Mr. Gleave so long as he remained medical officer to the lodge. (Applause.) Brother Gleave, who was c,,rdially received, replied in a feeling manner, and thanked the membare fur their kind- ness.

Brother A. Derbyshire proposed "Succees to the Runcorn district," which was responded to by Air. Jusepb theave, Junior, the district sLcretary. Brother Littler briefly gave the toast, "The Grand United Order of Oddlellowe."

Brother Harlem, D.G.lif , responded in are admirable speech dealing with many matters of interest to the order ; end be gave the members much valuable advice as to the conduct of their lodge. Alluding to the suggerion to es- ttblish a pension fund, he said the idea of the G.U.O. was to work the scheme in connection with the Puet-office euperane nu ation system, and they would thus have absolute govern. meet security. He mentioned the progress the order was making abroad, and concluded by wisting the Runcorn lodges every success. (Applause.) On the proposition of Brother Worthington, seconded by Brother Derbyshire, a vote of thanks was accorded Brother Earlam for his eloquent and instructive speech. The remainder or the evening was spent in a most enjoy- able manner. Brother Pollitt gave several humourous reci- tations, Brother Riley and. Brother Derbyshire gave read- ings, and songs were rendered by Brother Littler and Brother Thompson.
Tne proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chaiunin.

ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES. ' On Thursday night, at eleven o'clock, Francis Morgan, libeurer at Messrs. (hake'', Deacon; and Co.'s works, Wid- nes, met with an accident whilst following his employment. He was engaged in wheeling a barrow over sins liquor tanks, and, coining to a turn, be missed his footing and fell in, scalding himself severely in different parrs of his body. He was removed to the hospital and attended by Dr. ltl‘Cainbridge.—Yesterday morning an accident happened to a man named William Rogerson, who is also employed at the works of Messrs. Gasket', Deacon, and Co. tie was wheeling a barrow laden with lime across the yard, and fell on some railway metals, and before be could get out of the way some waggons, which were being drawn by a locomo- tive, °night the barrow and forced the shafts into R igerson's stomach. Ile was taken home, and it was found that he bad sustained a severe shock to his system, lie was atten- ded by Mr. Richards.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN. ‘g.p., AND A WARRINGTON UNIONIST. - IMPORTANT
LETTER.

A. Warrington Radical Unionist having for- warded certain extracts from Mr. Chamberlain's speeches which have been printed in this and other journals, with a view to showing that the member for West Birmingham has somewhat changed his attitude on the Irish question, Mr. Chamberlain ham replied as follows : Ilionnuny, Moon GIMEN, BraIIINGRAIL DXCEMBER 30m, 1886.

Dear Sir,—Mr. Chamberlain desires me' to ac- knowledge receipt of your letter of the 26th just, and extracts enclosed. He has previously dealt with a similar attempt to misrepresent his attitude on the Irish question, but he has little hope that anything that may be said will deter unscrupulous politicians from using any means, however unfair, to damage an opponent. The facts are, however, as follows :—ln the first, speech to which reference is made, Mr. Chamberlain was arguing in favour of a great extension of local government to Ireland. and he believes that the de- scription he then gave of the state of things in that country was perfectly accurate. _ . .

In tile speech delivered on July 6th, 1886, he re- ferred to the political and social advantages which are enjoyed by Irishmen to an equal extent with their fellow subjects in England, Scotland, and Wales, and he instanced Parliamentary representa- tion, religious equality, and land laws which afford greater security to property of Irish tenant farmers than to that of their fellow agriculturalists in other parts of the kingdom. In one respect only are they worse off than we in England are, namely, as re- gards a proper system of local government; and on this point Mr. Chamberlain has over and over again announced his readiness to support the largest pos- sible measure that is consistent with the mainten- ance of the supreme authority of the British Parlia- ment. It is, therefore, a wilful distortion of the, facts, when it is sought by means of incomplete- and misleading extracts from Mr. Chamberlain's. speeches, to show that his position in the present . controversy is inconsistent with the views he pre- viously advocated.—l am, yours truly, 'WILLIAM WooDINGs.

The Bulgarian Delegates on Thursday waited upon the Lord Mayor privately at the Mansion House, accompanied by the Seryian Consul-General. His Lordship Invited them to luncheon at the Mansion louse next Monday.

The Qaeen, accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Hattenherg, left Windsor Castle on Wednesday for Os- horne. Her Majesty has consented to Parliament being, further prorogued from tne 13th to the 27th of January. I INFANTILE MORTALITY.—The coroner for East Surrey I was • n Tuesday informed of the deaths of six infants in the parith-s of Newington, Bermondsey, and Rotherhitbe, who had been found desd in bud beside their mothers on Sunday and Monday mornings. MR. PARNELL'S tiIIALTEL—II is stated that Mr. rarnell has almost completely recovered from his gastric attack. but any excitement would expose him to the thing gof a re- lapse, and he will scrupulously abstain from all public speaking whilst in Ireland. FRIGHTFUL DEATIL—JamPs Hell, platelayer, while work- ing on the Lancashire and Yorkshire line near Liverpool. on Monday, 'yapped out of !the way of a goods train, but was knocked to the ground by the York express and killed, his body I:Pieg frightfully mutilated. SUSPBCTED SALE OF DISEASED MEAT.—At Dares- bury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Mary Emma Per- cival, farmer, Appleton, was summoned for having had in her possession on the 15th November a pig • which was suffering from swine fever, and having • failed to give notice of the existence of the disease. Sergeant Booth said on the 9th ult he received in- formation of a pig being at Mrs. Chantler's which was suffering from swine fever. On questioning Mrs. Chantler, he ascertained that a pig had been bought from Mrs. Percival, and at the time the pur- chase was made there was another pig in the stye which defendant's son said he would give her if she would take it home to nurse. She had the pig winch was ill taken home, and it died two days afterwards. The officer afterwards paid a visit to defendant's premises, as he had reason to suspect that swine fever existed there. He asked the defen- dant several questions, ELM ascertained that one or two pigs had died, and that one had been sold to a Warrington butcher. Mr. Ferguson gave evidence showing that he had made a post-mortem examina- tion of the carcase of a pig, and found that the animal had been suffering from swine fever for . four or five days before its death. He inspected , another pig whicli was in a stye, and found that it was suffering from the disease. In answer to the magistrates' clerk (Mr. Nicholson), defendant said she did not know the name of the Warrington " butcher to whom other pigs were sold. Her son knew who it was, but she did not. She had never seen swine fever, and did not know anything about the nature of the symptoms. The magistrates, con- _ sidering the case to be a bad one, imposed a penalty • of .f.,5 and costs. div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

THE MEMORIAL TO THE LATE BEY. CANON BARCLAY.—A fund has been opened for the purpose of raising a monu- ment to the late Vicar of Runcorn. Subscriptions may be paid to Mr. E. A. Chorlton, manager of Parr's Bank, or to any member of the committee. Full particulars may be gathered from our advertisement columns. RUNCORN POLLING Dtaratcr.—After the addresses, on Wednesday evening, in reference to Mr. Gladstone's birth- day. Mr. It. Shaw was appointed chairman of the Runcorn Polliag District, and Mr. J. R. Frith was appointed vice- chairman. The usual number of gentlemen were appointed to represent Runcorn on the Liberal Council of the Division.

PRESENTATION AT RIINCORN.—The services of Mr. John Holford, as choirmaeter to the United Methodist Free Church, Runcorn. have just been appropriately recognised by the congregation of that body. He has been made the recipient of an elegant silver-mounted ivory baton, the presentation having been made on behalf of the members by Mr. E. Gandy, the circuit secretary.

. . HOLY TRINITY DIVIDING CLUE, RONCORIL—This society has declared and paid a dividend of lie per member. At the annual meeting held recently Mr. w. 11. Roger- son, of Bridge-street, was the recipient of six volumes of Dr. Geikies " Hours with the Bible," in recognition of hi a services to the society as hon. treaeurer. Mr. W. Leathwood made the presentation on behalf of the mem- bers.

DEATH FROM SCALDS AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, on Friday held an inquest at the Widnes Police Court upon the body of Thomas loran, infant son of Patrick Horan, labourer, of 27, Lacey-street. The mother was preparing a bath for the baby and poured a quantity of hot water into a tub. Whilst she went to fetch some cold water, the child fell from the chair on which it was into the hot water, and was badly scalded. The accident occurred on the 21st October, and death ensued on the 23rd De-

cember. PIiIKAIINTATION AT WIDNES.-Mr. Walter H. Swinn, who for the past eight years has occupied a responsible position at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., has obtained the position of manager at the Greenbank Alkali Works, St. Helens. The regret of the office staff and the foreman at his approachimr departure, was appropriately show.n on Friday last, when they presented him with a tangible proof of their regard and esteem in the shape of a purse of gold. The presentation was made by Mr. George Pryde, a member of the firm, who in felicitious terms congratulated Mr. Swumn upon his appointment, and expressed hearty wishes for his future success,

TREAT TO NEWSBOYS AT WIDNBS.—Th9 annual treat to the Newsboys of Widnes, organised by Mrs. Morewood, newsagent, Widnes-road, widow of the late Mr. J. P. More- wood, reporter, took place on Monday evening. About 40 boys sat down to an excellent tea at the residence of Mrs. Morewood. who attended to their wants, assisted by Miss Latham (Manchester), Miss Rogerson, Miss Carlile, and Miss Morewood. Subsequently the boys were regaled with fruit, and a capital entertainment was given for the amuse- ment of the young guests. At the conclusion a vote of thanks was accorded to the subscribers to the treat fund, on the motion of Master W. B. Morewood, seconded by Master Barnett. The chief contributors to the f aria were Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P., Mr. J. Brock, J.P., Mr. Timmis, J.P., and Mr. Pankhurst.

Mary's Catholic Church. The church was decorated with ivy, holly, dm., the great attraction, however, being a representation of the Nativity of the Saviour, which was placed in the side chapel on the north side of the , church. Standing at the front of the crib the scene was very interesting. With the cavern stable the infant Saviour was seen lying on the straw in the ceotre.the Virgin , Mary kneeliegin adoration on one side, and St. Joseph on the other. The ex and the ass were seen in the back-ground, whilst in the far distance the hills of Bethlehem were distin- guished, the Star of the Eaet being also shown. On Christ-. mas day the masses commenced at half .past six in the morne ing, continuing every half-hour until half-past ten, during which time members of th• congregation were either enter- ing or leaving the church. The solemn high mass com— menced at eleven o'clock, the celebrant being the Rev. F. W. Sumner, 05.8.. the superior of St. Mary's, assisted by I Father Corlett as deacon and Father Carew as sub-deacon. The music of the masses was rendered by a full chair, and solos being taken by Miss Annie Burrows (treble), Mrs. Eccles (contralto), Meesrs. Henry Brown and Joseph Dolan I (tenors), and Messrs. Peter Mather and H. Eccles (bass). I The small organ was presided over by Mr. Mather, as usual ; while the choir were under the baton of Mr. R. Eccles. I There was no sermon. as is usual, on Christmas Day,, the service beingof great length. After the mess the prayer for the Queen, "Victoria Regina," was sung, during which the magnificent altar was illuminated for the benediction ser- vice, there being no evening service. The celebrant o? the mass then disrobed in the chancel, at the credence table, and I robed again with the vestments for benediction. The Sacred Host was then placed on the beautiful throne ef the altar, and the "0 ealutaria " sung by the choir. The tenor solo in the " Tantum ergo" wae sung by Mr. Henry Brown with his urinal ability. DINER TO POOR PEOPLL. Through the generosity of the ex-Mayor (Alderman Harrison) a large number of the poor people of the town were again supplied with a substantial Christrnae dinner at the Drill Hall. Mr. George Riley, the school attendance cer, was again entrusted with the distribution of tickets for the dinner to persons who might be considered proper recipients of Alderman Harrison's hospitality, and to the performance of this work much time and care were bestowed by Me. Biley and his assistant, Mr. W. Jones. In all, about 750 tickets were distributed to persons of ages ranging from the child barely able to walk to the veteran who had long been in the "sere and y-llow at"le of life. As a result, about noon on Christmas Day, the possessors ef tickets (locked to the Drill Hall in great numbers, the long rows of seats be- ing quickly occupied. In rot a few cases the whole of the members of a family owed their Christmas dinner to the ex- Mayor, and in other cases a number of the children were sent evidently to relieve the pressure on the scanty latder at home. The dinner consisted of "hotpot," made of beef and potatoes, and was plentiful in quantity, and savoury and nourishing in quality. SHOCKING MURDER AT KETTERING, NORTHAMPTON. sumg.—Con Christmas morning an old man named Osborne, who resided alone in a cottage at Kettering, Northampton- shire, was found dead en the floor of the sitting room, hie bead being shockingly cut and battered, and one of his fin- I gers being nearly severed. The floor and walls of the rcom were bespattered with blood, and Itbere were other indica- tions of a revere struggle. No one, however, appears tc have heard any disturbance, although the street is within 30 yards of the cottage, and numbers of people were Parad- ing the thoroughfare until late at night en Christmas Eve. , As the old man was in receipt of parish relief and was of a I quiet and inoffensive disposition, it i 3 difficult to surmise i the motive for the crime. THE ERA OF PEACE. Mr. E,ditor,—l want to know, do you know, whether you belong to the "Peace at any price party,' because if you do, or if say of your party belong to it, you must feel in high glee at the {VAT tt ings are going. What won&rful tales we have heard and read lately about wars. gore that would send out messengers of peace and good will by the ton, armour plates, foolishly invented by patriotic and disinterested Christian men, designed to Show that a wonderful resisting force there is in a lump of iron. How beautifully things work for the general good. We only want twenty new cruisers, with a few guns, that will drop dvnar.lite within an inch of them Russian, Ger- man, and Frerrh scamps, and how comfortable we shall feel. I'll tell yin what, Mr. Editor, I feeljeatisfied that the statement made by the "Daily Telegraph," of Nov. 13th, was as near correct as poesible. It said :—" The Queen's jubilee must have cast its sunshine before, just as some- times in spring we have a perfect summer day. for there never was a time in English politics when men and manners were so millenial." What do you think of that? Sir S. Clarke's "rumour of war" speech. Lord Charles Beresford'e dismal croakings, and all the efforts made by the War Office and Admiralty to make trade brisk down at Woolwich—what is it all? We are enjoying a "peef.ct sum- mer's day." We have it on the authority of the "D.T." By-the-way, these initials seem ominous, and perhaps the leaner with the largest circulation had been on the spree and got the " tremens," or else it would not have gone on to say :-0 The coming millenium has even touched the Irish shore, where events have fought on the side of conces- sion and compromise." Dear-a-me, a abort month ago and we had all the above blessed news given to us, and now to- day what do we hear? A heaven-born Tory Onvernment, with a Christian feeling, truly grand and beautiful, show- ing the Irish cotters the outside of their cabin doors, and there leaving them to study the beauties of nature as ex• hibited on their snow-clad mountains. Now thankful the Irish ought to be to the Tories, for what can be better for a country than to see the classes well provided with the good things of this earth. It mast be a pleasure to the masses to be allowed the triviledge of loading the rich man's table with Christmas dainties. But this happy Tory family with their staunch sup- porters, the Disunionists, bow elated they must be with the success of all their plane; the Radical Chamberlain drafting tills for the Democratic Churchill—what a eight. could a body have seen the faces of the "Old Gang" as they sat and listened to Lord Randolph as be sketched his County Board Bill, as be twisted his moustache and pretested against his Budget being made an ever-increasing quantity! I have -hopes yet. Mr. Editor, that we shall not be hurried into a general election for a while, because Lord Randolph refuses ' •to defend his country by spending a few more toppers. It -does not follow that no one else will. You know Mr. Glad- stone is to be kept from power at all cost. Well, Lord Randolph has gone—who can fill his place? 'lt was said two or three years ago that the Tories had -abundance of "dormant talent" amongst them. If it does rpot remain dormant why not make use of it now? Surely the Tories are not fast ; if they be, why not make use of the nice old gentleman whom the Warringtonians have ticketed, convict fashion, 501? He has a financial genius not at all •dormant, as is proved by the eteady growth of Wilderspool. Ah, well, Mr. Editor, I set out to talk about war and all its benefits ; but how can we have a glorious war if the ; 'Chancellor of the Exehrcmer refuses the First Lord's appli- cation for cash? It's preposterous; that young Democrat I ought to have gone about his in:mines" long ago. 'lt's my ; belief that he is to blame for Lord Salisbury having to tear I his hair, and the Berlin treaty in a lit of, well, the gout. I don't know of any other aristocratic fit. And I know the I Irish landlords look upon his lordship and General Buller -as two arch conepirators bent upon robbing them of their vents. How much better would it have been now had the Irish had a man prepared to carry out Salisbury's Newport speech? Why, Parnell, Dillon, and all the rest of the dis- satisfied tribe would now have been comfortably picking oakum; England would have been enjoying her "summer's day." Nay, I believe, but for that Randolph we should have had the whole world crouching at the feet of the Brit- ish Lion at this moment. We may accent it as ore of the.standard British truths, that Scotland, Wales, and Ireland, nay, sir, all the world outside this tight little island, most bend their necks beneath our heels, for are we not the pioneers of peace and of Christian truths? Are we not in the van of civilization? Oar might makes all things right, and so God save the Queen.

OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. Tutiastur. Last night Lord llttrtington arrived in London, in no genial temper as may be supposed, for, baying given up his contemplated journey to India in de- ference to the entreaties of his political friends, he thought he really had earned a few weeks holiday in southern Europe. But Lord Hartington proposed and Lord Randolph Churchill disposed. To-day the twin chief of the dissentient Liberals has met his co-partner, Mr. Chamberlain, and other members of the party. To-morrow he is to see Lord Salisbury and return an answer to the urgent appeal to "come over:and help us." No authoritative announce- ment has been made of the result of the meeting of the Liberal Dissentients, but it may, I think, with safety he assumed that Lord Hartington has resolved to decline the overtures made to him. It is difficult, in tiny circumstances, to imagine his taking any other course. He has not, that anyone is aware of, a special mission to save a Conserva- tive Government from impending dissolution. If , be were to take the Conservative shilling and don Ministerial unifornr of Conservative colours, he must make up his n.lnd to sit for the rest of his liferon the Conserratire•side of' the House. That Lord Hartington, with all his Whig propensities, is not prepared to do. iicthlis not been able to swal- low the proposal of Hortie•Rider; but apart from that,. lie is a stout Liberal, to .whom we should not Angel the party owes many' services in times past. But since Lord Salisburyin.the- earliest moment of desperation made plaintive appeal, to Lord Hart- ington the situation has consideraNY altered. Is is clear that Lord Hartingtonicould not alone joint the Conservative ranks. He mast take with him some of those who have in his company stood aloof from Mr.. Gladstone's leadership: That means the swamping; or at least the leavening:ofßoxiservative office holderswith Liberal recruita. If Lord Hart- ington takes,office with three or four of his friends, four or five of the gentlemen nowjanugily ensconced in office must' turn out. This they are not inclined to do, and aniagitation has been got up throughout the party, which s if Lord Hartington wean-more in- clined to take office than he is, would be sußcient to check him off: The Conservatives, threnigti their organs in the •Pfess,. frankly avow" thatithey are willing to receive•the fullest measne of help limn Lord Hartingtter,but be must not expect any-4th° loaves and fishes. Thus the mattes standrzto.-1114. The probable •retßnit will be that Lord Salisbury will have to stumble along with his Ministryreconi- structed trom wrthiu In the meantime the- meet- ing of Parliament; has been deferred tillCiumasy 27th.

There are many:versions current et:the precise circumstances that led, up to the resignntion Randolph Churchill. r happen to be personally:ay- quainted with some•of the parties to the • gunnei. and their intiniev;. and!havre heard the -Mots -statbdi with authority. It- all came about within a Iseek;. beginning from the return of Mr. Chamiterlain Ifrom. the Continent. Disclosures, had about Owl time been made by one of the London morning newepapers-of the decision of the Cabinet with respect to ,the• Local Government Bill. Mr. Chamberlren deem:tell that Lord Randolph ) hadlbeen outvoted du his adl vac.acy of the old bill, which was really Mn Chain+ berlain's, and which providbd for the establishment of county boards upon) purely elective principlbs.) On Saturday, the-18tb, Lord Randolph Ch'urchill; dined with Mr. Chamberlain, where this imittbr was discussed, and Mr.-Chamberlain plainly intimated to his guest that in the event of such a bil/ as. that. forecasted being brought jail* would himself move • its rejection. That, as Lord Randolph clearly perceived. meantk the defeat of the • Government upon a specifif ground which he could notlersonally defentkt ITe is, at bottom, as Radical as. Mr Chamberlain -hi—
imr-i

self, and honestly desired to see the vexed qpeetio of Local Government dealt with upon a democratic basis. He brooded over the matter till Monday Lunching out on Sunday, he talked portentously about resigning, but his friends, have been familia with such threata-almost since hesjoined tile Gev ' ernment—certainly since his Dartford speec-h,, andi. little attention was paid to' him. On- Monday he had an interview with Mr. 7ir. H. Smith, in which • he nearly frightened the life- out of that placid per- son by his remarks on the estimates. He next-wentT down to Windsor-in fulfilment of an engagement of old-standing, and thence wrote to Lord Salisbury stating his diffitulties aboat the estimates,. and,. assuming that the Premier would stand by the. fireo Lord of the Adraimlty and: the Minister for War, tendered his resignation. This Lord Salisbury, per-, haps sotnewhail to Lord. Eandolph's surprise,. ac cepted, and Lord Randolph wrote again, more -hilly vindicating his action. He-said nothing about-the Local Government Bill, but confined his arguments.l Ito the question of the estimates. This letter--Lord. Salisbury received at Hatfield by the last pest on Wedni3sday, and, putiing it+ in his pocket, Wen.t top, the ball Lady Salisbury was giving. Among • his, guests was Lord Randolph's mother, the Duchess. of Marlborough. But Lord Salisbury did not 'say a word to her or- even to his wife, and both ladies. were first 'mad accfuainted.with thelact'whenthey- read "The Tithes" next laming. ' . • Sir Henry Wolff, who is providentially in- town, and is buzziag about lit hi characteristicallytdiplo-. matic manner, is quite certain that if Lord' Ran- dolph had ; not committed his secret to ," The Times" the thing would have blown over. His ad- mission is that Lord Rautiolph resigned in a huff; believing-thut here, as has happened on former oc- casions, Lord Salisbury and his colleagues, would!, "cave in," • Sir Henry Wolff faintly believes that even yet reconciliation :nay take place. Pc de not find many people who share this belief. Lord i'mti- dolph burned his boatsand his bridges when he communicated to " Thee Times" the fact of his re- signation. T#4. wasr in- itself an imprecpdented proeeeding,:m uffison Intik the whole epiecide. • It is said,, and rarifWell be helieVed; that the-Qaeen„Who had bsgunrather to fancy the young Tory minister, is ftsperately angry with hid( fot what she regards as a slight paid to herself. The Queen, punctilious in all -ceremonious-matters, has an almost childish joalousy.for the maintenance of the fletion:that it is she who appoints ministries and dismisses minis- ters.. Till Lord Randolph had submitted his resigna- tion to her and receiyed her gracious -permission, to ,iesign, it was, according to Court theory, a physical 'impossibility that he-should be other than. Chancel:. lor of the Exchequer. Lord Randolph, in his frank and fractious manner, thrust his foot through this paper screen, and communicated the fact directly to the public; leavino the Queen to ascertain its ac- complishment from what is called in the House of Commons "the ordinary sources of intelligence." This is an escapade the Queen will never-forget or forgive.

"-The Times," which usually lags behind its con- temporaries, whether in town- or• country, with res- pect to special information, has been greatly uplifted by being seleCtod as`the niediura for the exclusive conveyance of this momentous 'intelligence. Per- haps it is not especially to tke credit of the mana- gers of the paper that they should be. able to print a State secret voluntarily communicated without any effort or manosvuring of their own. Where the cleverness of the managers of "The Times" came in was in the steps they took to keep the se- cret when once it tumbled into their mouths. Lord. Randolph Churchill drove into, Printing House Square shortly after eleven on Wednesday night, and asked to see the editor. He was lodged with him for nearly an hour, at the end of which time, lo! as Mr. Black says in his novels, a strange thing happened. As soon as Lord Randolph had been seen off the premises, an order was issued to lock every door back and front, and take the keys ot the editor's room. Despatches as they arrived through the night wee taken in at a window in the. court- yard. Not a soul, from the editor's rooni to the companionship of the printer's devil* was permitted

Bavonne Plut:—lilb potatoes, }lb turnips, fib onions, 2OM celery, 1 oz. tapioca, 14 oz. butter, 2 boiled eggs. I Boil the vegetables till nearly cooked with sufficient water to cover them, except the onion which is better fried to a light brown color, place the onion at the bottom of a pis dish, then a layer of the potatoes cut or broken in pieces, then the turelp and celery with the eggs cat into slices, sprinkle the tapioca over the whole surface, fill up the dish with the remaining popatoes : add some mushreom ketchup to the water in which the vegetables were bailed with pepper and salt to taste, pour the mixture over the pie add more water if required so as to three-parts fill the dish. Make a paste as follows :-1 lb of decorticated wheat meal, one, of butter, 1 to spoon full of baking powder, a little salt. Mix the powder and salt well with the meal, then rub in the butter; mix with 4 pint of cold water with a fork or spoon. Do not kneed it, place the same on the paate board or slab well floured, roll out lightly, fold in three. roll It again, if not sufficiently smooth, fold and roll it again, let it lay on the board belt an hour, then place on the pie dish in the usual way,bake in a moderately hot oven one hour. Cost Is 2d. 6 lbe potatoes, 5 lbe parsnips, cost N. Peng PUDDI3O.-2 lb. pastry flour, 1 lb bread crumbs, 1 lb raisins, stoned and cut a little, 1 lb of currants ilb raw sugar, 4 eggs, lb butter, 2 oze. mixed candied peel out in thin slices,and the grated rind if a lemon,one small teaspoon fall of salt, 4 a grated nutmeg. Mix all the dry ingredients after rubbing the butter in the flour; add the eggs well beaten with as much milk as required to make the whole into a thick batter. Boil in a buttered basin or mould five hours, serve with sweet mines. Cord 2s bd. Total cost of 3 course dinner 5.54 for 16 persons, or 44 per head. The total weight of material when cooked would be about 30Ibe or 141 b for each person. Thanking you in anticipation; I wish you and your readers all a prosperous New Year.
W. H. CHAPMAN, Gelber:to-street, Warrington. December 47 th. 1880.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. Limon onia OWN CORRISPONDNNT, 23. Old Broad-street, B.C. But for the settlement which commenced on Tuesday. the Stock Exchange might without the lust ineonYenience to anybody have extended the holidays for at least another day, as even the necessary business connected with Use set- tlement could not be carried on owing to the utter isolation into which London had been plunged; it was impossible to either receive or send a telegram, and for all practical pm, pases of prompt business the city might have been non- existent. A urines responsibility rests with the authorities in not making the whole telegraphic system Independent of any sudden change to which ear erratic climate is subject, and the demoralisation consequent upon this state of things was plainly visible on the Stock Exchange. Little or no business was done, and prices fell wherever a seller ap- peared. The making up prices en Wednesday were at the very worst, after which a general rebound took place. As an example of this, the making up price for settlement of Brighton A's was ill, on Thursday the price for buyers was 11n; the continuation rates have been almost unprece- dandy high, and the demand for money bas been met with rates equal to 1S to 20 per cent, per annum. Such is the momentary scarcity of money that brokers must pay any price to tide over the difficulties of settlement, and although there are announce- ments of a few failures, the last settlement of the year closes with a more cheerful feeling than was an- ticipated when members left for Christmas last week. Americans have generally ireprored since Wednesday. Home rails are more buoyant on the news of generally in- creased traffic returns of last week. My advice to holders not to be scared into selling by the collapse of prices a fort- night ago will be fully appreciated by those who acted upon it. To-day (Saturday) the Stock Exchange is closed as usual, being New Year's Day, and members will return next week in anticipation of a rise generally, if no serious difficulties crop up in the political world%

to leave the premises on any pretext whatever. For some hours mystery and consternation brooded over the establishment. The secret was till two o'clock in the morning locked in the breast of the editor and two leader writers. The paragraph an- nouncing the resignation, and the articles commen- ting thereon were written and held back to the last moment. But even then, the hour being one at which other papers had gone to press, the doors were stilllocked, and it was not till the paper had gone to priss that the doors were unlocked. This is "how they brought the news to Ghent," and how it was jealously kept there. Mr. Gladstone's birthday at Hawarden yesterday was kept in the ordinary fashion. It was hard lines for the local post office and postman. All the ends of the earth endeavoured to do the veteran states- man honour. Telegrams, letters, cards, and presents flowed in throughout the day. Never in the highest flights of success has Mr. Gladstone received fuller testimony of the esteem in which mankind holds him. I heard from a colleague who recently saw him that he is in the highest spirits, positively cer- tain that before six months are over he will again be Prime Minister,and carrying out the Irish policy, which has made ouch enormous strides since he first nailed it to the mast. Certainly the events of the past week do much to justify this hopefulness. Whether Mr. Gladstone will presently be strong enough to resume office may be a question. There is no question that the present Ministry have ro- ceived their death blow.

The most notable of these is the large statue of "St. Michael overcoming Sat*," in the Warrington Art Gallery. This wonderful work is the result of the public subscription of £l,OOO, which sum was placed at Mr. Wood's dis- posal to supply a suitable work of art for the new Art Gallery. Of this great work it has been said: "It must have required great courage on the part of a comparatively young artist to treat a subject on which the genius of a Flaxman had been exer- cised in the maturity of his powers; -but there was none of that 'vaulting ambition which doth o'erleap itself' in the selection of this subject on the part of Mr. Wood, and modest merit has triumphed in the successful treatment of a most difficult subject. Mr. Warrington Wood has also succeeded adnsirably in 'Satan vanquished,' which he modelled in clay and chiselled in marble. The winged figure of Michael is of colossal size, his face radiant with the calm of angelic majesty and supernal might ; in his right hand he carries a flaming sword, and with his left ho'ids down the vanquished foroof Satan, who writhes in hellish rage, beneath the superior prowess of the victorious Archangel'. The face of Satan is a powerful study, furrowed by the lints of mingled rage and misery at his fall, his, wings, in texture like a bat, feebly distendeded; his' body bent and crushed towards the earth by, his victor, all indicte his complete and utter defeat, The en- tire work is mentorious, its conceptisi;h design., composition, and execution being of that superior' order which ranks it as a work of high art." Ili the Warrington Art Gallery there are also torte subs- scription busts by Mr. Wood, one of Mr. V, Veto, moat, the first Mayor of the town, and the other' of the Rector, the Rev. W. Quekett. In the Town' Hall there are the admirable busts of Lord Winniarr.- leigh and Mr. George Crostield. Almost all the tradesmen litring in the streets traversed by the proces- sion hadtPartially closed their places, and at almost every :home there were blinds drawn, showing. the great respect in which the deceased gentleman was held. M the police had made excellent arrange- talents there was no stoppage of traffic in the streetn, and, the greatest decorum was observed, both during. the twogress through the town of the mournful pro- cession, and' nn its arrival at the cemetery. The•wsoffin, whieh was. of oak, was made by Mr. Hobert Garnett and Co.„Sankey-street, Warrington, and bore.on a brass plate , the inseriptinn—" John Warrington Wood, died December 26th, 11164, agent years? Wreaths that had been sent by soerl,eireg relatives and friends were platted' on the coffin, whioh, being in the chapel at the cemetery, was viewed by a large number of people. A short serTice was conducted in the chapel by the Rev. J. A. Drummond, on behalf of the Rector, by whom also, assisted by the Rev. D. Jenkins, the final ceremony at the grave was conducted. The feaeral arrangements were under the care of Messrs. J. and W. • Dutton, and were personally superintended by Dir. James Dutton.
The body of a man, name unknown, has been disoovered at Perth, Rhondda, frozen to death. .

Captain Child, of the Manchester Volunteer Battalion, was found dead in bed at Llandudno on Monday, At an inquest held at St. Thomas's Hospital on the body of Robert John Janawav, it wait, who was shot at Clapham by the landlord of the Rising Sun, the jury returned a ver- dict of death from misadventure.
_ Father Fatly, who was recently released from Galway gaol. WRS accorded an enthusiastic reception at Woodford, on Monday. He declared that he was prepared to make greater sacrifices for WS country.,

div.head: FRIGHTFUL COLOIERY ACCIDENT NEAR' BARNSLEY.• TEN MEN MUM._
div.p: FRIGHTFUL COLOIERY ACCIDENT NEAR' BARNSLEY.• TEN MEN MUM._

, . Bettiten nine and ten o'clock on' 'Thnsdy night caeoffthe most shockingtollieryeediaents,thrtMgh the breaking of a rope;*,which evitr'oheurred in .lOrkshfrii, took place, at the Houghton Maineol- Him new Barfield, about seven., miles from Barnsley... It seemed that 'a numbetbf men Were descending the shaft in the cage to 'commence to work the night shaft, when the rope attached to the cage 'broke, within fifty. yards fronarthe pit bot- temo andrecipitated the whole of the men to the ba'Aonyai the shaft, which is over 400 yards deep. Ten.of its'orcupants were killed on the-spot, their bodies being afterwards brought in a 'frightfully mutilated state to the pit bank, where they were laid test; and presented a mast shocking. spectacle. IThe Barnsley seam of coal is worked, .and about 400 men und.'.boys are employed at the coffiery. A Barnsley correspondent who paid a visit to the colliery on Friday morning, telegraph's -that the disasterii one of an appalling character, the bodies of the tan-inen being literally smashed. UT, td 'noon the dismenlbered remains were still lying mettle pit bottom. Theitilled. include a father and his two loons, entity/tither and one son. At ten minutes to eight o'clack lest night the draw of men who had completedAte,afternoon shift, were being raised to the bank ins% 'three-decked cage, the unfortunate victinis of thedfsaster occupying the top deck: The engine tentanAnen.Beresford, of Snape Hllll. Par- field, states 'that when the cage was withia 150 yards of the surface he heard a crack on the tep of the drum. 11* *ms instantly struck across theefore- head by a piece 'Off wood, and rendered insensible. By the time her-recovered his senses "the job was done." The appearance of the roof of the engine house, which is to .w great extent smashed in; favours the idea that tire cage end its occupants were drawn to the top an& precipitated down the shaft 535 yards deep.lPart °Utile sliding gates on the pit hill, which protect the shaft, are also canied mtorthe headgear. OverrfiVehundred men are employed at the colliery. Atrthe time of the accident 135 men were in the workings, and were drawn outrby another shaft: the men killed are financial members of the West Riding Miners' Permanent Fund.

Fletcher and Sons' colliery,. at Ratcliffe, when about :Iwo tons of roof fell from a pothole on the father, break- ing both his legs and severely injuring his chest, causing instant death.

Peter Nelson, a collier, aged 'fit); was forced against a tub, the ironwork of which pierced his left sidb three inches, causing instan- taneous death. To other colliers were injured:

THE MINISTER/AL CRISIS. 4 INTERVIEW BETWEEN LORD SALISBURY" - AND ,LOAD, HARTINGTON. The Central News says Lord Salisbury arrived in Arlington-street from -Hatfield at noon on Fridny, and was engaged with his secretaries until' one o'clock, when he received a visit from Lord Fflirt- ington, who had previously conferred ato Devon- shire House with Colonel Hozier' Mr. Courtenay, and Mr. Goschen. Shortly before two Lord Hftrt- higton left Arlington-street and proceeded' to brooks Club. where- he lunched. About the same time the Premier drove to the Athaneum Club r and !remained there until three o'clock, at which hr he proceeded to Downing-street and had interviews with Lord Rowton and the Turkish Ambasaador. Meanwhile Lord Hdrtington had met Mr. Gosellen at Brooks' Club, and conversed with him until nearly four o'clock; when his lordship proceeded' to Devonshire House with Mr. Chamberlain, whornshe had met on the way.

The conference between Lord Hartington- end Lord Salisbury on• Friday afternoon lasted jnet one hour. We have reason to believe that the conver- satron between' the, two statesmen was by no means confined' to the question of ' the Liberal Unioniat leader taking office.. Indeed Lord Salisbupy- 'had already been, made aware of Lord Hartington's decision, and the Premier to-clay received thealaditional information that Mr. Goschen was not disposed to join the Cabinet: The desirableness of Making certain Con- cessions to Lord R. Churchill in order to induce him to re-enter the Cabinet was referred to. only how- ever to be promptly dropped as inexpedient, and unpracticable. The chief topics of conversation were the foreign policy a the Government •in re- gard to which the Liberal Unionist-leaders particu- larly desiredrinformation in view of the sensational statementh on the subject recently published. and the . financiattand' legislative programmed the Government. Lord Hartington while cordially dis- posed to gite the Government an active support in the•coming session required information and ex- planation 4 on, the foregoing subjects in order to 'satisfy the wishes of certain of his colleagues whose assistance is not to be implicitly relied upon as his own, except upon the great' queStltlh of HOmeßule. We are in a position to state that Lord Salisbury's exp.lanation , to the Liberal Unionist leader was. eminently satisfactory. SHUFFLING THE CARDS.

Lora Salisbury will proceed' to reconsti uct hi Cabinet, and he will have completed his arrange- mentscrobably by Wednesday -next, after which Ile will commence a series of Cabinet Councils. At present there is no indicatiomthat the Premier.will abandon his original intention of offering the'posi- tion vacated by Lord R. Churchill to Mr. W. IT. Smith.

The Press Association hears that although Mr. Smith will in all probability be the new leader of the House of Commons, he will retain, his post as Secretary of State for War, while the new Chancel- lor of the Exchequer -will be Mr. Stanhope. A vacancy will thus be caused at tbe,Colonial Office, :and this, it is rumoured, will be:filled by Lord Car- 'narvori, who will once more enter a Conservative Cabinet, 4 , Lord Randolph Churdhill makes no. effort to con- ceal the fact that he is open to terms. If Lord Iddes/eigh and Lord Cross are dismissed he will return to the fold. This suggestbm has caused n great deal of irritation in CO neervative circles.
